note: Space Travel (round 14, DATA_DECISIONS section 74). EDITORIAL: this file is the source of truth for /space/travel. Bump `version` when you edit it; never hand-edit data/space/travel/*. The `spacetravel` stage validates every entry, downloads every image through the free-licence gate and writes the artifacts; scripts/check-spacetravel.mjs gates the result.
sourcingPolicy: Every figure carries the source actually consulted and the year it was consulted or published. Agency pages (NASA, NSSDCA, ESA, CNSA, ISRO, SpaceX) are preferred; where the figure is only tabulated encyclopaedically, the Wikipedia article that was read is cited by name rather than dressed up as an agency source. A figure a source does not publish is null WITH a reason and renders as "not available" -- never zero, never an estimate passed off as a measurement. Facts dated after June 2024 were re-checked against live sources on 2026-10-10 (the assistant's knowledge cutoff is earlier than this file's vintage); where a live check could not confirm a date, the entry says so or was left out.
imageNote: Every photograph, drawing and portrait on this page was downloaded at build time and is served from this site -- nothing is hotlinked. Sources are NASA (and other US-government) public-domain media and Wikimedia Commons files that passed a free-licence gate (public domain, CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA, Attribution; never NC or ND). Each image carries its own credit and licence.
eraNote: These eras are threads, not a strict partition of the calendar. Robotic exploration, the station era and the commercial present all run in parallel; each event is filed under the thread it belongs to, and the dates on the banners overlap on purpose.

eras.label: The idea
eras.summary: Space travel was a story before it was an engineering problem. Satire, then astronomy, then fiction imagined the voyage; between 1903 and 1933 Tsiolkovsky, Oberth, Goddard and the amateur rocket societies turned it into mathematics, hardware and a plan.

eras.label: Rockets of war
eras.summary: The first rocket that could reach space was a weapon. Germany's A-4/V-2 was built by concentration-camp prisoners and fired at cities; more people died making it than were killed by it. In 1945 both the United States and the Soviet Union took its engineers, its drawings and its hardware home.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum - Mittelbau-Dora

eras.label: The first satellites
eras.summary: On 4 October 1957 a 58-centimetre aluminium sphere began beeping overhead and the space age started in earnest. Within four years satellites had found the radiation belts, photographed the far side of the Moon and been built in half a dozen countries -- and the Soviet chief designer who made it possible was still a state secret.

eras.label: Humans in orbit
eras.summary: Five years took human flight from one orbit in a sphere to two-week missions, spacewalks, rendezvous and docking. Vostok, Mercury, Voskhod and Gemini were flown while the techniques they needed were still being invented.

eras.label: The Moon
eras.summary: Robots crashed, then landed, then drove and brought samples home; twelve people walked on the surface between 1969 and 1972. The race had a losing side, and it lost in public silence: the Soviet N1 failed four times and the lunar programme was cancelled.

eras.label: Stations and shuttles
eras.summary: After the Moon, the destination became orbit itself: Salyut, Skylab, Mir, the International Space Station and Tiangong, served by a reusable spaceplane that never became cheap and twice killed its crew.

eras.label: Robotic explorers
eras.summary: Everything else in the Solar System has been visited by machines. Flybys became orbiters, orbiters became landers, landers became rovers and sample-return capsules -- and two 1977 spacecraft are still transmitting from interstellar space.

eras.label: The present
eras.summary: Orbital rockets now land and fly again; crews reach the station in commercial capsules; three countries fly their own astronauts and a fourth is close. The Moon is a destination again, the station that defined the last quarter-century has an end date, and the largest rocket ever flown reached orbit for the first time in September 2026.

plates.title: Launch vehicles, to scale
plates.intro: Nineteen launch vehicles drawn to one scale, from the 14-metre weapon that started it to the 121-metre stack that reached orbit in September 2026. Each outline is generated from that vehicle's published stage lengths and diameters -- nothing here is traced by hand or stretched to fit.
plates.note: Heights are as the operator or agency publishes them, which is not a single convention: for most vehicles the figure includes the payload fairing or the spacecraft, while Saturn IB's published 43.2 m is the launch vehicle alone (with an Apollo spacecraft on top the stack stood about 68 m). The scale bar and the two reference figures are the only things on the plate that are not a vehicle. The Space Shuttle and Energia carry their orbiters in SIDE ELEVATION, as they sit on the stack, so the wings are seen edge-on; the orbiter's full 23.79 m span is on the crewed-spacecraft plate. Widths across strap-on boosters are composed from the published core and booster diameters, with the boosters drawn against the core they are bolted to.

plates.title: Crewed spacecraft, to scale
plates.intro: Thirteen vehicles that have carried, or are built to carry, people -- drawn nose-up as they sit on the launch vehicle, at one scale. The jump from Vostok's 2.3-metre sphere to Starship is the whole history of the subject in one picture.
plates.note: Lengths are the spacecraft's own, excluding the launch vehicle and the launch escape tower. The Space Shuttle orbiter and Starship are drawn nose-up because that is how they launch; their wings and fins are at their published spans.

plates.title: Space stations, to scale
plates.intro: Five crewed stations at one scale, seen broadside, with their mass, pressurised volume and usual crew. Fifty years separate the first from the largest; the ISS is longer than a football pitch is wide and still holds about as much air as a Boeing 747's cabin.
plates.note: Modules are drawn at their published lengths and diameters; solar arrays at their published spans. Station geometry changes with every visiting vehicle and reconfiguration -- each outline is the configuration named in its reference drawing, not a snapshot of any one day.

plates.title: Satellites and telescopes, to scale
plates.intro: From a 165-millimetre grapefruit to a sunshield the size of a tennis court. Seven spacecraft at one scale, spanning sixty-four years of satellite building.
plates.note: GPS Block IIF is in the catalogue but not on this plate: Boeing publishes the satellite's mass and design life but not its dimensions, and a spacecraft whose size is not published cannot honestly be drawn to scale.

craft.name: V-2 (Aggregat 4)
craft.summary: The first guided ballistic missile and the first human-made object to reach space, on a test flight in June 1944. It was series-produced by concentration-camp prisoners at the Mittelwerk underground factory, where more people died building it than were killed by it in action.

payloadLeoKg.why: The V-2 was a ballistic missile, not an orbital launcher: it threw a 1,000 kg warhead about 320 km down range, peaking near 90 km.

enginesText.v: 1 x ethanol/liquid-oxygen motor, 25 tonnes of thrust

drawing.title: V-2 rocket diagram (Commons, derived from the US Army technical manual)

craft.name: Sputnik (R-7 8K71PS)
craft.summary: A stripped-down version of the R-7 intercontinental missile, flown twice to launch Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2. Its layout -- a core stage surrounded by four tapering strap-on boosters, all lit on the ground -- is still flying today as Soyuz.

enginesText.v: Core 1 x RD-108, boosters 4 x RD-107 (20 chambers in all)

drawing.title: NASA RP-1357, Soviet launch vehicle drawings (public domain)

craft.name: Vostok-K
craft.summary: The R-7 with a third stage, rated to carry a person. It launched Yuri Gagarin, Valentina Tereshkova and every other Vostok cosmonaut.

enginesText.v: Core RD-108, four RD-107 boosters, third stage RD-0109

drawing.title: NASA RP-1357, Soviet launch vehicle drawings (public domain)

craft.name: Atlas LV-3B (Mercury-Atlas)
craft.summary: A converted intercontinental missile with a stainless-steel balloon tank so thin it had to be kept pressurised to stand up. It put the four orbital Mercury astronauts into space.

heightM.note: with the Mercury spacecraft and escape tower

enginesText.v: 2 x XLR-89 booster and 1 x XLR-105 sustainer (1,517 kN total)

drawing.title: NASA Mercury-Atlas launch vehicle drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Titan II GLV
craft.summary: A hypergolic-fuelled missile adapted for Gemini. All twelve flew successfully, and because the propellants ignited on contact there was nothing to light and nothing to fail at ignition.

enginesText.v: 1 x LR87-AJ-7 (first stage), 1 x LR91-AJ-7 (second stage)

drawing.title: NASA Gemini-Titan II launch vehicle drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Saturn IB
craft.organisation: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center / Chrysler, Douglas
craft.summary: A cluster of eight engines under a tank assembly welded from Redstone hardware, topped with the hydrogen stage that would later fly to the Moon. It launched Apollo 7, the three Skylab crews and the Apollo-Soyuz mission.

heightM.note: launch vehicle without payload; with an Apollo spacecraft the stack stood about 68 m

enginesText.v: 8 x Rocketdyne H-1 (first stage), 1 x J-2 (S-IVB)

drawing.title: NASA Saturn IB vehicle drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Saturn V
craft.organisation: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center / Boeing, North American, Douglas, IBM
craft.summary: The most powerful rocket to fly a successful mission for half a century, and still the only one to have carried people beyond Earth orbit. Thirteen launched; none failed.

heightM.note: with the Apollo spacecraft and escape tower

enginesText.v: 5 x F-1 (S-IC), 5 x J-2 (S-II), 1 x J-2 (S-IVB)

drawing.title: NASA Saturn V cutaway, unlabelled version (public domain)

craft.name: N1
craft.summary: The Soviet Moon rocket: thirty engines in its first stage, no all-up ground test stand, and four launches that all failed -- the second destroyed its own pad. The programme was suspended in 1974 and admitted to only in 1989.

enginesText.v: 30 x NK-15 (Block A), 8 x NK-15V, 4 x NK-21

drawing.title: NASA RP-1357, Soviet launch vehicle drawings (public domain)

craft.name: Proton-M
craft.organisation: Khrunichev State Research and Production Space Center
craft.summary: The current version of Vladimir Chelomei's UR-500, designed in the early 1960s as a missile and flown ever since as a heavy launcher -- the rocket that lifted Salyut, Mir's modules and the ISS's Zarya and Zvezda.

flights.v: in service; final launches planned by 2029

enginesText.v: 6 x RD-275M (first stage)

drawing.title: Khrunichev Proton-M payload user's guide drawings

craft.name: Space Shuttle (full stack)
craft.organisation: NASA / Rockwell International, Thiokol, Martin Marietta
craft.summary: A reusable spaceplane bolted to a throwaway tank and two solid boosters: the only crewed vehicle with wings ever flown operationally, and the only one that could return large cargo from orbit. It flew 135 missions and lost two crews.

diameterM.note: quoted stack width; the orbiter's wingspan is 23.79 m

enginesText.v: 3 x RS-25 on the orbiter, 2 x solid rocket boosters

drawing.title: NASA Space Shuttle vehicle illustration (public domain)

craft.name: Energia
craft.summary: A 100-tonne-to-orbit heavy lifter built around the RD-170, still the most powerful liquid rocket engine ever flown. It launched twice: once with a failed military payload, once with the Buran orbiter, and then the Soviet Union ended.

enginesText.v: 4 x RD-0120 (core), 4 x RD-170 (boosters)

drawing.title: NASA RP-1357, Soviet launch vehicle drawings (public domain)

craft.name: Ariane 5 ECA
craft.summary: Europe's heavy lifter for a quarter of a century. Its maiden flight blew up 37 seconds after launch; it went on to fly 117 times, delivering Rosetta, BepiColombo, JUICE and -- with a precision that added years to the telescope's life -- the James Webb Space Telescope.

heightM.note: up to 53 m depending on fairing

payloadLeoKg.why: ESA publishes Ariane 5 ECA performance to geostationary transfer orbit (10,865 kg), not to low Earth orbit; the launcher was not marketed for LEO delivery.

enginesText.v: 1 x Vulcain 2 (core), 2 x P241 solid boosters, 1 x HM7B (upper stage)

drawing.title: Arianespace Ariane 5 user's manual drawings

craft.name: Long March 5
craft.organisation: China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology (CALT)
craft.summary: China's heavy lifter, and the vehicle that made the rest of the Chinese programme possible: the Tiangong modules, the Chang'e 5 and 6 sample returns and the Tianwen-1 Mars mission all rode on it.

enginesText.v: 2 x YF-77 (core), 8 x YF-100 (four boosters), 2 x YF-75D (upper stage)

drawing.title: CALT Long March 5 user's manual drawings

craft.name: Soyuz-2.1a
craft.summary: The R-7's living descendant, with digital flight control. The same four-booster silhouette Korolev's bureau drew in 1954 is still the most-launched orbital rocket layout in history.

enginesText.v: 1 x RD-108A (core), 4 x RD-107A (boosters), 1 x RD-0110 (third stage)

drawing.title: Arianespace Soyuz user's manual drawings

craft.name: Falcon 9 Block 5
craft.summary: The first orbital-class rocket to land and fly again, and now the most-flown operational launcher in the world. One booster had flown 37 times by August 2026.

payloadLeoKg.note: expendable; 17,500 kg when the booster lands on a droneship

flights.v: in service; one booster has flown 37 times (August 2026)
flights.src: Space.com / Wikipedia, List of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launches

enginesText.v: 9 x Merlin 1D (first stage), 1 x Merlin 1D Vacuum (second stage)

drawing.title: SpaceX Falcon User's Guide drawings

craft.name: Falcon Heavy
craft.summary: Three Falcon 9 first stages side by side, twenty-seven engines at liftoff. Its first flight carried a car; since then it has launched Psyche, Europa Clipper and the first Gateway modules' heavy predecessors.

enginesText.v: 27 x Merlin 1D at liftoff, 1 x Merlin 1D Vacuum (second stage)

drawing.title: SpaceX Falcon User's Guide drawings

craft.name: Space Launch System Block 1
craft.organisation: NASA / Boeing, Aerojet Rocketdyne, Northrop Grumman
craft.summary: NASA's Moon rocket, assembled largely from Shuttle propulsion: four flight-proven RS-25 engines and two five-segment solid boosters. It has flown twice -- Artemis I uncrewed in 2022, Artemis II with four astronauts in April 2026.

enginesText.v: 4 x RS-25 (core), 2 x five-segment solid rocket boosters

drawing.title: NASA SLS Block 1 reference drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Starship / Super Heavy
craft.summary: The tallest and most powerful rocket ever flown: 33 Raptor engines under a stainless-steel booster designed to be caught by its own launch tower. After eleven suborbital test flights it reached orbit for the first time on 28 September 2026 and deployed 26 Starlink satellites.

heightM.note: Block 1 stack; Block 2 is 123.1 m and Block 3 124.4 m

payloadLeoKg.note: Block 2; 100 t and 200 t are stated goals for later blocks, not demonstrated

flights.v: 14 test flights; first orbital flight 28 September 2026

enginesText.v: 33 x Raptor (Super Heavy), 3 x Raptor + 3 x Raptor Vacuum (Starship)

drawing.title: FAA Starship/Super Heavy internal structure drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Electron
craft.summary: A carbon-composite small launcher with electric-pump-fed engines and 3D-printed combustion chambers -- at 18 metres, the smallest rocket on this plate and the busiest dedicated small-satellite launcher in service.

payloadLeoKg.note: 200 kg to a 500 km Sun-synchronous orbit

enginesText.v: 9 x Rutherford (first stage), 1 x Rutherford Vacuum (second stage)

drawing.title: Rocket Lab Electron payload user's guide drawings

craft.name: Vostok
craft.summary: A 2.3-metre pressurised sphere -- the easiest shape to make strong and the only one whose re-entry attitude looks after itself. The cosmonaut was ejected and parachuted separately, and the capsule hit the ground hard enough that the flights were described carefully to the world's record-keepers.

diameterM.note: the crew sphere is 2.3 m across

pressurisedVolumeM3.why: No official pressurised-volume figure is published for the Vostok descent sphere.

drawing.title: Vostok spacecraft diagram (Commons, CC BY-SA)

craft.name: Mercury capsule
craft.summary: Max Faget's blunt-ended cone: so small the astronauts said you did not get into it, you put it on. Six crewed flights, two of them suborbital, with 2.8 cubic metres of habitable volume -- about the inside of a telephone box.

drawing.title: NASA Mercury spacecraft cutaway (public domain)

craft.name: Voskhod
craft.summary: A Vostok with the ejection seat taken out so that two or three people could be squeezed in, and -- on its second flight -- an inflatable airlock taped to the hatch for the first spacewalk. Both flights were improvisations to stay ahead of Gemini.

drawing.title: NASA Voskhod crew seating cutaway (public domain)

craft.name: Gemini
craft.summary: The spacecraft that learned how to fly: ten crewed missions in twenty months taught NASA rendezvous, docking, spacewalking and a fortnight in orbit -- everything Apollo needed and nothing it could do without.

massKg.note: heaviest flown; the lightest was 3,220 kg

drawing.title: NASA Gemini spacecraft artist concept (public domain)

craft.name: Apollo Command and Service Module
craft.summary: The mothership: a three-seat cone with 5.9 cubic metres of living space, bolted to a service module whose single engine had to work to get anyone home from the Moon. Nine CSMs flew to the Moon and all nine came back.

diameterM.src: Wikipedia, Apollo command and service module

massKg.src: Wikipedia, Apollo command and service module

crew.src: Wikipedia, Apollo command and service module

pressurisedVolumeM3.src: Wikipedia, Apollo command and service module

enginesText.src: Wikipedia, Apollo command and service module

drawing.title: NASA cutaway of the Apollo 10 spacecraft, S69-34072 (public domain)

sources.title: Wikipedia, Apollo command and service module

craft.name: Apollo Lunar Module
craft.summary: The first and still the only crewed vehicle designed to fly nowhere but in vacuum: no aerodynamics, no paint, walls in places as thin as a drinks can. Six of them landed two people each on the Moon, and a seventh kept the Apollo 13 crew alive.

diameterM.note: across the deployed landing gear; the ascent stage is 4.29 m across

drawing.title: NASA Apollo Lunar Module diagram 0101207 (public domain)

craft.name: Soyuz MS
craft.summary: The longest-serving crewed spacecraft in history, flying since 1967 in continuously revised form. Its first flight killed Vladimir Komarov and its first station crew died on the way home in 1971; after those two disasters it became the most reliable crew ferry ever built.

drawing.title: NASA Soyuz-TMA descent module drawing, unlabelled (public domain)

craft.name: Shenzhou
craft.summary: China's crew ferry: Soyuz-like in layout, larger, with its own orbital module that can fly free. Shenzhou 5 made China the third country to launch a person on its own rocket in 2003; the type now rotates crews to Tiangong.

drawing.title: Tiangong configuration drawing with Shenzhou attached (Commons, CC BY-SA)

craft.name: Space Shuttle orbiter
craft.summary: A 37-metre delta-winged spaceplane with a 18.3-metre cargo bay and a robot arm -- the only spacecraft that could launch a satellite, repair it, and bring another one home. Five flew; two were destroyed with their crews.

heightM.note: length; drawn nose-up because that is how it launched

diameterM.note: wingspan; the orbiter stands 17.86 m tall on its gear

crew.note: two flight crew plus up to five others

drawing.title: NASA Space Shuttle orbiter illustration (public domain)

craft.name: Crew Dragon
craft.summary: The first privately built spacecraft to carry people to orbit, and since 2020 the United States' only crew ferry. Its abort engines are built into the capsule wall rather than a tower, so it can escape at any point in the climb.

heightM.note: with trunk; the capsule alone is 4.5 m

crew.note: up to seven in an emergency configuration

drawing.title: SpaceX Dragon payload user's guide drawings

craft.name: Orion
craft.summary: Apollo's shape, scaled up and rebuilt for deep space, with a European service module derived from the ISS cargo ships. It flew uncrewed around the Moon in 2022 and carried four astronauts round it in April 2026.

massKg.note: crew module with European Service Module

silhouette.heightNote: Composed, not a single published figure: the 3.3 m crew module (NASA) plus the 4.0 m European Service Module (ESA). No agency publishes one stack height for the pair.

drawing.title: NASA Orion spacecraft reference drawings (public domain)

craft.name: Boeing Starliner (CST-100)
craft.summary: The second Commercial Crew vehicle. Its crewed test flight in June 2024 lost five of eight manoeuvring thrusters on approach to the station; NASA judged a crewed return too risky and brought the capsule back empty, leaving its two astronauts to come home on a Dragon.

massKg.why: Boeing does not publish a launch mass for the Starliner stack.

crew.note: designed for up to seven; NASA flies four

drawing.title: Boeing Starliner reference drawings

craft.name: Starship (upper stage)
craft.summary: The upper stage of the Starship system, flown alone to orbit for the first time in September 2026 and selected by NASA as the Artemis lunar lander. Fifty-two metres of stainless steel -- taller than the whole Mercury-Atlas stack.

crew.why: No crewed Starship configuration has flown or been published in detail; SpaceX states a goal of up to 100 people per flight, which is an intention rather than a specification.

flights.v: 14 test flights; first orbital flight 28 September 2026

enginesText.v: 3 x Raptor and 3 x Raptor Vacuum

drawing.title: FAA Starship internal structure drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Salyut 1
craft.summary: The first space station. One crew managed to get inside, for 23 days; all three died when their Soyuz lost its atmosphere during re-entry. The station was deliberately destroyed four months later.

flights.v: 1 crew aboard (Soyuz 11); Soyuz 10 failed to dock hard

drawing.title: NASA RP-1357 Salyut 1 drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Skylab
craft.organisation: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center / McDonnell Douglas
craft.summary: A Saturn V third stage converted into a house: 351 cubic metres, the roomiest station ever flown until the ISS. It lost its meteoroid shield and one solar wing during launch, and the first crew had to repair it before they could move in.

drawing.title: NASA cutaway view of the Skylab orbital workshop, 0101589 (public domain)

craft.name: Mir
craft.summary: The first modular station, assembled over ten years from seven pressurised modules and occupied for twelve and a half of its fifteen years. It survived a fire and a collision, hosted American astronauts from 1995, and taught everyone how to run a station for the long term.

drawing.title: Mir configuration diagram (Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0, Orionist)

craft.name: International Space Station
craft.country: United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, Canada
craft.summary: The largest structure ever assembled off Earth: 109 metres across, about a thousand cubic metres of pressurised volume, continuously crewed since November 2000. Operations are funded to the end of 2030, after which a purpose-built SpaceX vehicle is to bring it down over an empty stretch of ocean.

lengthM.note: overall; the truss alone is 94 m

drawing.title: NASA ISS configuration diagram, December 2022 (public domain)

craft.name: Tiangong
craft.summary: China's three-module station, completed in November 2022 and permanently crewed since June 2022. About a fifth of the ISS's mass, with its own laboratories, airlock, robot arm and a free-flying survey telescope planned to share its orbit.

lengthM.note: across the station with visiting vehicles

flights.v: Tianhe 2021, Wentian and Mengtian 2022; crewed continuously since June 2022

drawing.title: Tiangong configuration 2022 (Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, Shujianyang)

craft.name: Sputnik 1
craft.summary: The first artificial satellite: a polished aluminium sphere 58 centimetres across, pressurised with nitrogen, carrying two radio transmitters and nothing else. Its beeping could be picked up by amateurs anywhere on Earth, which was the point.

spanM.note: longest of the four swept-back antennas; two were 2.4 m and two 2.9 m

silhouette.spanNote: Composed from the published sphere diameter and antenna lengths: the four antennas swept back from one hemisphere, so the overall extent is not itself a published figure.

drawing.title: Sputnik 1 schematic (Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0)

craft.name: Explorer 1
craft.organisation: Jet Propulsion Laboratory / Army Ballistic Missile Agency
craft.summary: The first American satellite, and the first to make a discovery: James Van Allen's cosmic-ray detector found the radiation belts that now carry his name. Fourteen kilograms, and the fourth stage of its launcher stayed attached as part of the spacecraft.

drawing.title: NASA Explorer 1 characteristics drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Vanguard 1
craft.summary: A 1.46-kilogram, 165-millimetre sphere -- the fourth satellite ever launched, the first to run on solar cells, and the oldest human-made object still in orbit. Its radio went silent in 1964; the body will stay up for centuries.

flights.v: transmitted until May 1964; still in orbit

silhouette.spanNote: Composed from the published 165 mm sphere and its six 300 mm antennas.

drawing.title: NASA NSSDCA Vanguard 1 description and drawing (public domain)

craft.name: Telstar 1
craft.summary: The first commercial communications satellite and the first to relay live television across the Atlantic. It worked for seven months before radiation from high-altitude nuclear tests -- including one conducted the day before its launch -- destroyed its transistors.

drawing.title: NASA NSSDCA Telstar 1 description (public domain)

craft.name: Hubble Space Telescope
craft.summary: A 2.4-metre telescope above the atmosphere, launched with a mirror ground to the wrong shape and fixed in orbit three years later. Five Shuttle servicing missions rebuilt it piece by piece; it has been observing for more than thirty-five years.

silhouette.spanNote: Body at the published 13.2 m length and 4.2 m diameter; the solar-array proportions are measured from the cited NASA cutaway drawing, which is the only published view of their extent.

drawing.title: NASA Hubble instruments cutaway (public domain)

craft.name: James Webb Space Telescope
craft.summary: A 6.5-metre segmented infrared mirror behind a five-layer sunshield the size of a tennis court, folded to fit inside an Ariane 5 and unfolded over two weeks a million and a half kilometres from Earth. Three hundred and forty-four single-point failures had to work. They all did.

flights.v: operating at the Sun-Earth L2 point since 2022

drawing.title: NASA JWST optical layout, unlabelled version (public domain)

craft.name: Starlink V2 Mini
craft.summary: A mass-produced internet relay, built at a rate of several a day and launched by the dozen. The constellation it belongs to numbered roughly ten thousand working satellites in mid-2026 -- more spacecraft than the rest of history put together.

spanM.note: with both solar wings deployed, approximately

drawing.title: SpaceX Starlink V2 Mini press imagery

sources.title: Spaceflight Now, SpaceX unveils first batch of larger upgraded Starlink satellites

craft.name: GPS Block IIF
craft.summary: Twelve navigation satellites, each carrying atomic clocks accurate enough that relativity has to be corrected for. Satellite navigation is the piece of space infrastructure almost everyone uses daily without noticing.

spanM.why: Boeing publishes the satellite's mass and design life but not its dimensions or solar-array span, so it is not drawn on the scale plate.

craft.name: Luna 1
craft.summary: The first spacecraft to leave Earth's gravitational grip. It missed the Moon by about 6,000 kilometres and became the first human-made object in orbit around the Sun, after releasing a cloud of sodium gas that could be photographed from the ground.

flights.v: first flyby of the Moon and first object in heliocentric orbit

craft.name: Luna 3
craft.summary: It photographed the far side of the Moon on film, developed the film on board, scanned it with a flying-spot scanner and radioed the pictures home. Twenty-nine frames, grainy beyond belief, of a hemisphere no one had ever seen.

flights.v: first photographs of the lunar far side

craft.name: Luna 9
craft.summary: The first soft landing on another world. An airbag-cushioned capsule the size of a beach ball bounced to rest in Oceanus Procellarum and sent back panoramas showing that the surface would bear a spacecraft's weight -- which had been a genuine open question.

flights.v: first soft landing on the Moon, 3 February 1966

craft.name: Luna 16
craft.summary: The first robotic sample return from another world: it drilled 35 centimetres into Mare Fecunditatis, sealed 101 grams of soil in a capsule and flew it back to Kazakhstan while Apollo was still flying.

craft.name: Lunokhod 1
craft.summary: The first rover on another world: a bathtub on eight wire-mesh wheels, driven from Earth by a five-person crew reading slow television pictures. It covered 10.5 kilometres in ten lunar days.

flights.v: first roving vehicle on another world

craft.name: Mariner 4
craft.summary: The first close look at Mars, in July 1965: 21 pictures of a cratered, apparently dead surface, taken as the spacecraft swept past at 9,800 kilometres. They ended a century of speculation about canals and vegetation in one afternoon.

craft.name: Venera 7
craft.summary: The first spacecraft to transmit from the surface of another planet. It lasted 23 minutes on Venus and measured 475 degrees Celsius and 90 atmospheres -- a world no lander has survived for longer than a couple of hours since.

flights.v: first transmission from the surface of another planet

craft.name: Viking 1
craft.summary: The first spacecraft to land on Mars and work: it photographed the surface for six years and ran three biology experiments whose results are still argued about. Its orbiter mapped the planet at a resolution nothing bettered for twenty years.

craft.name: Pioneer 10
craft.summary: The first spacecraft through the asteroid belt and the first to reach Jupiter, in December 1973. It carried the engraved plaque showing two human figures and the Sun's position among fourteen pulsars, and it is still coasting outward.

craft.name: Voyager 1
craft.summary: The most distant human-made object: about 25.9 billion kilometres away in November 2026, in interstellar space since 2012, still returning magnetic-field and plasma-wave data on a few watts. Instruments are being switched off one at a time to stretch the power out.

distanceKm.src: NASA, Where Are Voyager 1 and 2 Now?

flights.v: crossed into interstellar space in 2012; operating

sources.title: NASA, Where Are Voyager 1 and 2 Now?

craft.name: Voyager 2
craft.summary: The only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune, in 1986 and 1989, on a planetary alignment that will not repeat for 175 years. It crossed into interstellar space in 2018 and is still transmitting from over 21 billion kilometres.

distanceKm.src: NASA, Where Are Voyager 1 and 2 Now?

flights.v: flybys of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; interstellar since 2018

craft.name: Galileo
craft.summary: The first Jupiter orbiter, and the only spacecraft to have dropped a probe into a giant planet's atmosphere. Its main antenna never opened, so fourteen years of science came home through a low-gain antenna at a few hundred bits per second.

flights.v: deliberately destroyed in Jupiter's atmosphere, 21 September 2003

craft.name: Cassini-Huygens
craft.summary: Thirteen years in orbit around Saturn, and the only landing ever made in the outer Solar System: ESA's Huygens probe reached Titan's surface in January 2005. Cassini was flown into Saturn at the end so that it could never contaminate Enceladus.

massKg.note: at launch, including Huygens and propellant

flights.v: Saturn orbit 2004-2017; Huygens landed on Titan 14 January 2005

craft.name: Sojourner
craft.summary: The first wheels on Mars: an 11-kilogram rover carried inside an airbag-cushioned lander, driving a few metres a day and proving that a cheap mission could do real geology.

craft.name: Spirit and Opportunity
craft.summary: Two 185-kilogram rovers sent for 90 days each. Spirit lasted six years; Opportunity lasted fourteen and drove 45 kilometres, finding the mineral evidence that Mars once had standing water.

craft.name: Curiosity
craft.summary: A nuclear-powered, car-sized laboratory lowered onto Mars by a rocket-powered crane in 2012. It has been climbing a five-kilometre mountain of layered sediment ever since, reading the planet's climate history upward through the rock.

craft.name: Perseverance
craft.summary: Curiosity's successor, exploring a river delta in Jezero crater and sealing rock cores in titanium tubes for a return mission that has not yet been funded. It also made oxygen from the Martian atmosphere, in grams, for the first time.

craft.name: Ingenuity
craft.summary: A 1.8-kilogram helicopter sent to prove that powered flight was possible in an atmosphere one percent as thick as Earth's. It was meant to make five flights; it made 72 over three years, and ended with a damaged rotor blade.

craft.name: New Horizons
craft.organisation: NASA / Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory
craft.summary: The fastest spacecraft ever launched from Earth, and the only one to have visited Pluto: a single July 2015 flyby that turned a blurred dot into a world with nitrogen glaciers. In 2019 it flew past Arrokoth, the most distant object ever examined close up.

craft.name: Rosetta and Philae
craft.summary: The first spacecraft to orbit a comet and the first to land on one. Philae's harpoons failed, so it bounced twice and came to rest in shadow, working for 60 hours on batteries; Rosetta followed the comet for two years and then set itself down on it.

craft.name: Hayabusa2
craft.summary: It fired a copper slug into asteroid Ryugu to make a fresh crater, landed twice, and returned 5.4 grams of pristine material to the Australian desert in December 2020 -- then set off for another asteroid with the fuel it had left.

flights.v: capsule returned 6 December 2020; extended mission continues

craft.name: OSIRIS-REx
craft.summary: It touched asteroid Bennu for five seconds, blew nitrogen gas into the surface to stir up material, and brought 121.6 grams of it home to Utah in September 2023 -- the largest sample returned from beyond the Moon. The spacecraft flew on to asteroid Apophis.

craft.name: Chang'e 4 and Yutu-2
craft.organisation: CNSA / China Academy of Space Technology
craft.summary: The first landing on the far side of the Moon, in January 2019. Because the far side never faces Earth, the mission needed a relay satellite parked beyond the Moon to talk to it at all. The Yutu-2 rover is still driving.

massKg.note: lander; the Yutu-2 rover is 140 kg

flights.v: landed in Von Karman crater, 3 January 2019

craft.name: Chang'e 6
craft.organisation: CNSA / China Academy of Space Technology
craft.summary: The first sample return from the far side of the Moon: 1,935.3 grams scooped and drilled from the South Pole-Aitken basin and landed in Inner Mongolia on 25 June 2024. The samples come from the oldest, deepest impact structure on the Moon.

sources.title: CNSA, China's Chang'e-6 collects 1,935.3 grams of samples from the Moon's far side

craft.name: Chandrayaan-3
craft.summary: India's Vikram lander touched down near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, four years after its predecessor crashed, making India the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first to reach that latitude. The Pragyan rover worked for one lunar day.

massKg.note: lander including the 26 kg Pragyan rover

flights.v: landed 23 August 2023; operated one lunar day

craft.name: Europa Clipper
craft.organisation: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory / Johns Hopkins APL
craft.summary: The largest spacecraft NASA has built for a planetary mission, on its way to make nearly fifty close passes of Europa and work out whether the ocean under its ice could support life. It reaches Jupiter in 2030, after gravity assists at Mars and Earth.

people.name: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky
people.bio: Deafened by scarlet fever at nine and largely self-taught, Tsiolkovsky spent his working life teaching mathematics in provincial Kaluga and his spare time working out, on paper, how spaceflight would have to be done. His 1903 paper gave the rocket equation that still governs every launch: the speed a rocket can reach depends on its exhaust velocity and the logarithm of its mass ratio, which is why rockets are mostly propellant and why they have stages. He proposed liquid oxygen and hydrogen as propellants, multistage boosters, airlocks, orbital stations and greenhouses in space, decades before any of it was built. In 1911 he wrote the line that became the motto of the whole enterprise: Earth is the cradle of humanity, but one cannot live in a cradle forever.

people.name: Robert H. Goddard
people.bio: Goddard built what Tsiolkovsky calculated. On 16 March 1926, on his aunt's farm at Auburn, Massachusetts, he launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket: it flew for two and a half seconds and reached 12.5 metres. He went on, mostly alone and mostly in the New Mexico desert, to invent and patent gyroscopic steering, gimballed nozzles, pumped propellant feed, parachute recovery and the multistage rocket -- 214 patents in all, many of which every modern launcher infringes in spirit. Ridiculed by a New York Times editorial in 1920 for suggesting a rocket could work in vacuum, he worked in deliberate obscurity thereafter and published little. The Times printed a correction in July 1969, the day Apollo 11 left for the Moon.

people.name: Hermann Oberth
people.bio: Oberth's doctoral dissertation on rocket flight was rejected as utopian, so he published it himself in 1923 as Die Rakete zu den Planetenraeumen -- The Rocket into Interplanetary Space. It argued, with numbers, that a liquid-fuelled rocket could leave Earth, carry people and be made economic, and it created a generation of German rocket enthusiasts almost single-handedly. He was technical adviser on Fritz Lang's film Frau im Mond, mentored the teenage Wernher von Braun in the amateur Verein fuer Raumschiffahrt, and later worked briefly on the V-2 programme and, after the war, for the US Army at Huntsville. He lived to watch the Apollo 11 launch as a guest of his former student.

people.name: Herman Potocnik (Noordung)
people.bio: An invalided Austro-Hungarian officer writing under the pen name Hermann Noordung, Potocnik published one book -- The Problem of Space Travel: The Rocket Motor, in 1928 -- and died of pneumonia the next year, aged 36. In it he laid out the first engineering design for a space station: a rotating wheel generating artificial gravity by spin, with a parabolic solar mirror for power, a separate observatory and machine room, airlocks, cable-connected modules and spacesuits for maintenance. He also worked out that a satellite at about 35,900 kilometres would hold station over one point on the equator -- the geostationary orbit that every weather and television satellite now uses. Almost every space-station drawing of the next thirty years, von Braun's included, descends from his.

people.name: Sergei Korolev
people.bio: The most consequential engineer of the space age, and for most of his life a state secret: Soviet reports credited his work to an anonymous Chief Designer, and his name was published only in his obituary. Arrested in Stalin's purge of the aviation industry in 1938, he was sentenced to ten years, worked in a Kolyma gold mine, lost his teeth and nearly his life, and was transferred to a prison design bureau before release in 1944. He then built the R-7, the world's first intercontinental missile and still the ancestor of the Soyuz rocket, and used it to launch Sputnik 1, the dog Laika, the first Luna probes, Gagarin, Tereshkova and Leonov. He was managing the Soyuz spacecraft and the N1 Moon rocket when he died during routine surgery in January 1966, after which the Soviet lunar programme never recovered.
knownFor: R-7 and the Soyuz rocket family
Vostok and the first human spaceflight

people.name: Valentin Glushko
people.role: Chief designer of rocket engines, OKB-456 / NPO Energia
people.bio: If Korolev built the rockets, Glushko built almost everything that burned inside them. Arrested in the same 1938 purge and made to work from a prison design bureau, he went on to design the RD-107 and RD-108 engines that lifted Sputnik and Gagarin and still fly on Soyuz, and later the RD-170, the most powerful liquid rocket engine ever flown. He and Korolev fought for decades over propellants -- Glushko favoured storable hypergolics, Korolev wanted kerosene and oxygen for crewed flight -- and the quarrel cost the Soviet Moon programme its engine supplier, pushing Korolev to Nikolai Kuznetsov instead. After Korolev's death Glushko took over the bureau, cancelled the N1 and built Energia and Buran in its place.
knownFor: RD-170, the most powerful liquid engine flown

people.name: Vladimir Chelomei
people.bio: Korolev's chief rival inside the Soviet system, and a formidable political operator -- he hired Khrushchev's son and won work accordingly. His bureau designed the UR-500, which as Proton has been the Soviet and Russian heavy launcher for sixty years, lifting every Salyut, every Mir module and the first two ISS modules. He also designed the Almaz military space stations, which flew as Salyut 2, 3 and 5 with cosmonaut crews and a cannon, and the heavy TKS ferry whose pressurised module became the basis of Mir's and the ISS's Russian segments. His own crewed lunar flyby project, the UR-700 and LK-1, was cancelled in favour of Korolev's.
knownFor: TKS module design used on Mir and the ISS

people.name: Mikhail Yangel
people.bio: The third of the Soviet rocket chiefs, based at Dnipropetrovsk, responsible for the storable-propellant missiles that became the Kosmos and Tsyklon launchers and, later, the Zenit stage whose RD-170-powered boosters flew on Energia. On 24 October 1960 his R-16 missile exploded on the pad at Baikonur during a rushed pre-launch repair, killing the strategic rocket forces' commander-in-chief Marshal Nedelin and at least 78 others; Yangel survived because he had stepped away to smoke. The disaster was kept secret for nearly thirty years. He is included here as a designer whose work is largely invisible in the West but whose rockets launched hundreds of satellites.
knownFor: R-16 and the Kosmos and Tsyklon launchers

people.name: Vasily Mishin
people.bio: Korolev's long-time deputy, who inherited the Soviet lunar programme in 1966 without Korolev's political authority to defend it. Under Mishin the N1 flew four times and failed four times, Soyuz 1 killed Vladimir Komarov, and the Soyuz 11 crew died returning from Salyut 1; he was dismissed in 1974 and the N1 was cancelled. He also oversaw the Salyut programme's first stations and, after the Soviet collapse, published diaries that became a primary source on how the Moon race was actually run and lost. The engineering failures were real; so was the system that gave him a Moon rocket with no money for a test stand.
knownFor: Soyuz and the first Salyut stations
Diaries documenting the Soviet lunar programme
people.portraitNote: No free-licensed portrait of this person could be found.

people.name: Mikhail Tikhonravov
people.bio: The man who convinced the Soviet rocket establishment that an artificial satellite was both possible and worth doing. Tikhonravov's group worked out the packet-of-rockets staging arrangement that became the R-7's four-booster layout, and from 1950 he argued publicly -- against official indifference -- for an Earth satellite. When permission finally came he led the team that designed Sputnik 1 and, with Korolev, the Vostok capsule. He had also designed the first Soviet liquid-fuelled rocket to fly, in 1933, with the GIRD amateur group.
knownFor: The packet staging concept behind the R-7
GIRD-09, the first Soviet liquid rocket (1933)

people.name: Georgy Babakin
people.bio: When Soviet robotic planetary work was transferred from Korolev's overloaded bureau to Lavochkin in 1965, Babakin took it over and turned a record of failure into the most successful run of robotic firsts in the programme's history: Luna 9's first soft landing on the Moon, Luna 16's first robotic sample return, the Lunokhod rovers, Luna 17 and 21, and the Venera landers that first transmitted from the surface of Venus and survived its 475-degree heat. He died of a heart attack at 57, two years into that run; the bureau's planetary work continued under his name.
knownFor: Luna 9, the first soft lunar landing
Luna 16 sample return and the Lunokhod rovers

people.name: Nikolai Kuznetsov
people.bio: An aviation turbine designer who took on the N1's engines after Glushko refused to build kerosene-oxygen motors for it. His NK-15, and the improved NK-33, were the most efficient kerosene engines of their generation, and the reason the N1's first stage needed thirty of them was that nothing bigger was available. When the programme was cancelled Kuznetsov was ordered to destroy the remaining engines and instead had about ninety of them hidden in a warehouse; they were rediscovered in the 1990s, sold to American companies and flew decades later on the Antares rocket.
knownFor: Engines that flew 40 years after they were built

people.name: Wernher von Braun
people.role: Technical director, Peenemuende; director, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center
people.bio: The most capable rocket engineer of his generation and the most compromised. Von Braun joined the German Army's rocket programme in 1932, the Nazi Party in 1937 and the SS in 1940, rising to Sturmbannfuehrer, and as technical director at Peenemuende he led the development of the V-2 ballistic missile. The missile was series-produced at the Mittelwerk underground plant using concentration-camp prisoners from Mittelbau-Dora; von Braun visited the plant and, by his own later admission, saw the conditions, and he requested skilled prisoner labour. Around 20,000 prisoners died building the weapon -- more than it killed when fired. Surrendering to the Americans in 1945, he was brought to the United States under Operation Paperclip, built the Jupiter-C that launched Explorer 1, directed the Marshall Space Flight Center, led the team that designed the Saturn V, and became the public face of American spaceflight. Both halves of that record are his.

people.name: Arthur Rudolph
people.bio: Rudolph ran V-2 production. As operations director of the Mittelwerk plant he was directly responsible for the use of concentration-camp labour there, and a 1945 US intelligence report called him a menace to security and an ardent Nazi; he was brought to America anyway under Operation Paperclip. At NASA he was project director of the Saturn V, managing the programme that put Apollo on the Moon, and received the agency's Distinguished Service Medal. In 1984, facing a Justice Department investigation into his wartime record, he renounced his American citizenship and left for West Germany rather than contest denaturalisation. He is in this list because the Saturn V's management history cannot be told honestly without him.
knownFor: Renounced US citizenship in 1984 under investigation

people.name: Maxime Faget
people.role: Chief engineer, NASA Manned Spacecraft Center
people.bio: Faget designed the shape of American spaceflight. Working at Langley in the 1950s he proposed the blunt-body ballistic capsule -- a cone with a wide ablative heat shield, stable enough to re-enter nose-first without active control -- and that single decision defined Mercury, which he designed in detail, then Gemini and the Apollo command module. He held the patent on the Mercury capsule. As engineering director at the new Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston he shaped Apollo's spacecraft, argued for the lunar module's separate landing stage, and later led the design studies that produced the Space Shuttle orbiter. Colleagues described him as the man who could sketch a spacecraft on a napkin that still worked twenty years later.
knownFor: The blunt-body capsule and the Mercury spacecraft
Gemini and the Apollo command module

people.name: John Houbolt
people.bio: Houbolt worked out that the only affordable way to the Moon was to leave most of the spacecraft in lunar orbit and send down a small, separate lander -- lunar-orbit rendezvous. The idea was unpopular: NASA's leadership preferred either a direct ascent on an enormous rocket or assembly in Earth orbit, and rendezvous around the Moon with no abort option frightened people. Houbolt went outside the chain of command, writing directly to the associate administrator in 1961 to argue the arithmetic, and was eventually heard. Apollo flew his way, and the Saturn V exists at the size it does because of it.

people.name: Thomas J. Kelly
people.bio: Called the father of the lunar module, Kelly led Grumman's design of the first crewed vehicle built to operate only in vacuum. Everything followed from weight: no aerodynamic shape, no seats, no paint, walls of the ascent stage in places as thin as three sheets of foil, windows cut to triangles, and a cabin the crew flew standing up. The ascent engine had to be simple enough that it could not fail, because there was no backup and no rescue. Six of his landers brought twelve people off the Moon, and a seventh served as a lifeboat for the Apollo 13 crew.

people.name: George Low
people.role: Apollo Spacecraft Program Manager; NASA Deputy Administrator
people.bio: Low took over Apollo's spacecraft after the Apollo 1 fire killed three astronauts on the pad, and rebuilt both the command module and the programme's safety culture -- a new hatch that opened outward in seconds, non-flammable materials, and a redesigned interior. In August 1968, with the lunar module running late, it was Low who proposed sending Apollo 8 around the Moon instead of waiting: a decision taken in four months that produced the first human flight to another world. He later served as NASA's deputy administrator and oversaw the start of the Shuttle and the Apollo-Soyuz mission.
knownFor: Rebuilding the Apollo command module after the 1967 fire

portrait.title: Portrait of George M. Low - LRC-1970-B701 P-01270

people.name: George Mueller
people.role: NASA Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight
people.bio: Mueller made Apollo fit the decade. Arriving in 1963 to find a schedule that could not be met, he imposed all-up testing: instead of flying each Saturn V stage separately, every stage would be live on the first flight. Von Braun's engineers thought it reckless; it saved years, and the first Saturn V worked. He also installed the programme-management discipline, with its configuration control and formal reviews, that let half a million people build one machine. He went on to push Skylab -- built from leftover Apollo hardware -- and the Space Shuttle, and is often called the father of both.
knownFor: All-up testing of the Saturn V

people.name: Margaret Hamilton
people.role: Director of software engineering, MIT Instrumentation Laboratory
people.bio: Hamilton led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for the Apollo command module and lunar module, and coined the term software engineering to insist that the work was a discipline rather than an afterthought. She argued for error-detection and recovery code that management thought unnecessary -- astronauts would not make mistakes -- and built it anyway. Minutes from the first Moon landing, Apollo 11's computer began throwing 1202 alarms as it was overwhelmed by spurious radar data; because her software could shed low-priority tasks and keep the landing guidance running, the computer recovered instead of failing, and Armstrong and Aldrin landed. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.
knownFor: Asynchronous priority scheduling that saved the Apollo 11 landing

people.name: Katherine Johnson
people.bio: Johnson calculated trajectories for American spaceflight for three decades, beginning in the segregated West Area computing unit at Langley, where Black women mathematicians worked in a separate building with separate facilities. She computed the trajectory for Alan Shepard's 1961 suborbital flight and co-authored the report that put the equations for orbital flight into the open literature. When Langley's new electronic computers produced John Glenn's orbital numbers in 1962, Glenn asked that she check them by hand before he would fly. She went on to work on Apollo's lunar rendezvous calculations and the Shuttle, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015.

people.name: Mary Sherman Morgan
people.bio: The only woman among nine hundred engineers at North American Aviation's rocket division, and the one handed the problem of how to get more performance out of the Redstone without redesigning the engine. Her answer was Hydyne, a blend of unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine and diethylenetriamine that burned hotter than the alcohol fuel it replaced. It powered the first stage of the Jupiter-C that launched Explorer 1, America's first satellite, in February 1958. She had no degree, published nothing and was named in no press release; her work is known mainly because her son wrote it down.
knownFor: The Jupiter-C first stage that launched Explorer 1
people.portraitNote: No free-licensed portrait of this person could be found.

people.name: Qian Xuesen
people.role: Founder of the Chinese missile and space programme
people.bio: Qian co-founded the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, held a named professorship at Caltech and worked on American jet and rocket propulsion through the 1940s. In 1950, during the Red Scare, his security clearance was revoked on an unproven accusation of communist sympathies; he spent five years under effective house arrest and was deported in 1955. China made him the architect of its missile and space programmes: the Dongfeng missiles, the Long March launcher lineage descended from them, the 1970 Dong Fang Hong 1 satellite and the human spaceflight programme that became Shenzhou all trace to his organisation. A former US Navy undersecretary later called the deportation the stupidest thing the country ever did.
knownFor: Dongfeng missiles and the Long March lineage

people.name: Vikram Sarabhai
people.role: Founder of the Indian space programme
people.bio: A cosmic-ray physicist from an industrialist family, Sarabhai founded the Physical Research Laboratory at 28 and, after Sputnik, persuaded the Indian government that a poor country had more need of space technology than a rich one -- not for prestige, he argued, but for communications, weather forecasting and resource surveys. He set up the Thumba equatorial launching station in a fishing village, where the first rockets were carried to the pad on bicycles, and founded the organisation that became ISRO in 1969. He died at 52, before any of it flew.
knownFor: Space technology for development, not prestige

people.name: Satish Dhawan
people.bio: An aerodynamicist who took over ISRO after Sarabhai's death and ran it for a decade, delivering the SLV-3 launcher, the first Indian satellites and the remote-sensing and communications programmes that justified the whole enterprise domestically. He is remembered in Indian engineering as much for one gesture as for the hardware: when the first SLV-3 launch failed in 1979 he faced the press himself and took the blame, and when the next one succeeded he sent his project director to accept the credit. India's launch centre at Sriharikota is named after him.
people.portraitNote: No free-licensed portrait of this person could be found.

people.name: Tom Mueller
people.bio: Mueller built amateur liquid rocket engines in a garage with the Reaction Research Society before becoming SpaceX's first propulsion hire and its fifth employee. He led the design of the Merlin engine, which in its vacuum and sea-level forms powers every Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy flight and has become one of the most-flown rocket engines in history, and then of the methane-fuelled Raptor used by Starship. Merlin's combination of a simple gas-generator cycle, deep throttling and restart capability is what makes booster landing possible: the engine that lifts the rocket is the engine that lands it.
knownFor: Propulsion that made booster landings possible
people.portraitNote: No free-licensed portrait of this person could be found.

people.name: Gwynne Shotwell
people.role: President and Chief Operating Officer, SpaceX
people.bio: A mechanical engineer by training, Shotwell joined SpaceX as its seventh employee in 2002 and has run its commercial and day-to-day operations ever since, as president and chief operating officer. Her contribution is not a drawing but an operating model: the contracts and launch cadence that turned reusability from a demonstration into a business, the Commercial Crew and Commercial Resupply bids that made a private company NASA's crew carrier, and the production discipline behind launching more often than the rest of the world combined. She is listed here because the engineering of modern spaceflight is inseparable from the economics that pay for it.
knownFor: Turning booster reuse into an operating business

portrait.title: Gwynne Shotwell at 2018 Commercial Crew announcement

people.name: Peter Beck
people.role: Founder and chief executive, Rocket Lab
people.bio: Beck built rocket engines in his parents' shed in Invercargill and went on to found, in a country with no space industry at all, the first private company to reach orbit from the southern hemisphere. Electron's distinctive choices are his: a carbon-composite airframe, and the Rutherford engine, whose turbopumps are driven by electric motors and batteries rather than a gas generator, with combustion chambers printed rather than machined. Rocket Lab became the second most frequent American orbital launch provider, serving the small-satellite market that the big launchers treated as an afterthought.

events.title: Lucian writes the first voyage to the Moon
events.text: In A True Story the Syrian satirist Lucian of Samosata sends a ship up a waterspout to the Moon, where his crew joins a war between the Moonites and the people of the Sun. It is a parody of travellers' tales rather than a prediction, but it is the first surviving narrative of people leaving the Earth -- and it establishes a habit that lasted eighteen centuries: space travel was literature long before it was engineering.

image.title: William Strang spider battle in 1894 True History

events.title: Kepler's Somnium imagines the Moon as a place
events.text: Johannes Kepler wrote Somnium -- The Dream -- as a device for explaining Copernican astronomy: an Icelandic narrator is carried to the Moon by demons and describes the Earth as seen from there, moving in the sky. It is the first work to treat another world as a physical environment with its own gravity, seasons and inhabitants rather than a destination for allegory, which is why Carl Sagan and others have called it the first science-fiction novel.

events.title: Cyrano de Bergerac proposes going up by rocket
events.text: In Comical History of the States and Empires of the Moon, published posthumously in 1657, Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac's narrator tries dew-filled bottles and beef marrow before succeeding with a machine driven by rows of firework rockets, ignited in stages. It is a joke, but it is the first time anyone in print reaches space by the one method that actually works, and the first appearance of staging.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Comical History of the States and Empires of the Moon

events.title: Jules Verne fires three men at the Moon from Florida
events.text: From the Earth to the Moon launches its crew from a 270-metre cannon in Florida, works out the escape velocity and the free-fall weightlessness of the coast, and brings the capsule down in the Pacific where a US Navy ship recovers it. The acceleration would have killed everyone aboard instantly, but the book put the arithmetic of a Moon shot in front of a mass readership, and a century later Apollo 11 launched from Florida and splashed down in the Pacific.

image.title: From the Earth to the Moon Jules Verne

sources.title: Wikipedia, From the Earth to the Moon

events.title: Tsiolkovsky publishes the rocket equation
events.text: In The Exploration of Cosmic Space by Means of Reaction Devices, a deaf provincial schoolteacher set out the mathematics that governs every launch since: the velocity a rocket can gain equals its exhaust velocity times the logarithm of the ratio of its starting mass to its final mass. The consequence is brutal and unavoidable -- a rocket must be almost entirely propellant -- and it is why every vehicle on this page has stages it throws away.

events.title: "Earth is the cradle of humanity"
events.text: In a letter published in 1911 Tsiolkovsky wrote that the Earth is the cradle of humanity, but that one cannot live in a cradle forever. The sentence has been quoted ever since as the argument for the whole enterprise -- by Soviet propagandists, by NASA administrators and by commercial rocket companies, each meaning something different by it. He meant it literally: he expected humanity to spread through the Solar System in settlements powered by sunlight.

events.title: Oberth's book creates a generation of rocket engineers
events.text: Rejected as a dissertation, Die Rakete zu den Planetenraeumen was published privately and argued in detail that liquid-fuelled rockets could reach orbit, carry people and eventually pay for themselves. It sold, was argued over, and produced the amateur societies out of which the professional rocket programmes of three countries grew. Oberth was later technical adviser on Fritz Lang's Frau im Mond, which invented the countdown as a piece of dramatic timing.

events.title: The first liquid-fuelled rocket leaves the ground
events.text: On a snow-covered farm at Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert Goddard launched a spindly frame of pipes burning petrol and liquid oxygen. It rose 12.5 metres in two and a half seconds and crashed 56 metres away. Every orbital launch vehicle since has used the same principle, and Goddard went on to patent gimballed nozzles, gyroscopic steering, pumped propellant feed and staging -- the complete toolkit, worked out largely alone.

events.title: The amateurs: the VfR and its rocket field
events.text: The Verein fuer Raumschiffahrt, the German Society for Space Travel, was founded in 1927 by enthusiasts who had read Oberth. On a disused ammunition dump outside Berlin they flew the Mirak and Repulsor rockets, learned to handle liquid oxygen without killing themselves, and ran out of money in 1933. Their most promising teenage member, Wernher von Braun, had already taken a job with the German Army, which had funds the society did not.

events.title: Potocnik designs a space station
events.text: The Problem of Space Travel, written by a dying Slovene engineer under the name Hermann Noordung, contains the first engineering design for a crewed station: a rotating wheel spinning to make artificial gravity, a parabolic mirror for solar power, modules on cables, airlocks, and the observation that a satellite at about 35,900 kilometres altitude would stay above one point on the equator. Every space station ever drawn owes it something.

image.title: Noordung's Space Station Habitat Wheel - GPN-2003-00101

sources.title: Wikipedia, The Problem of Space Travel

events.title: A film invents the countdown
events.text: Fritz Lang's silent epic Frau im Mond had Hermann Oberth as technical adviser and a real rocket planned as a publicity stunt. Its multistage vehicle, water-tank launch pit and crew couches were close enough to the eventual reality to be uncomfortable, and the backwards count to launch -- invented for suspense -- was adopted by actual rocket crews and has never been dropped.

events.title: The Soviet amateurs fly GIRD-09
events.text: The Group for the Study of Reaction Propulsion, GIRD, was the Moscow counterpart of the German society -- unpaid, improvising, working in a cellar. Mikhail Tikhonravov's GIRD-09, burning jellied petrol and liquid oxygen, reached about 400 metres on 17 August 1933. Among its members were Tikhonravov, Valentin Glushko and a young aircraft engineer named Sergei Korolev; within four years the group had been absorbed into the state and its people would build the first satellite.

events.title: The German Army buys the rocket
events.text: Von Braun went to work for the German Army's ordnance branch in 1932, and from 1937 the programme had its own research establishment at Peenemuende on the Baltic coast, with thousands of staff and a budget no amateur society could approach. Its purpose was a ballistic missile with a one-tonne warhead and a range of 300 kilometres. The engineering was brilliant, the funding came from a rearming dictatorship, and the two cannot be separated.

image.title: Peenemunde test stand VII
image.credit: British Sortie N/853[2] by Flight Lieutenant R. A. Lenton and Sergeant R. S. Haney[3] took this photograph of Peenemünde, which shows 'a thick vertical column about 40 feet high' southeast of the 'buttresses':  Flight Lieutenant Andre' J. A. Kenny's Industrial Section[4] enlarges the photos and initially fails to identify the rocket.  Over a year later on August 4, 1944, Dr. R. V. Jones obtained a private set of the June 12, 1943 Peenemünde photos from the Medmenham commander, Group Captain P. G. Stewart, the 'thick vertical columns' were measured again and confirmed as vertical rockets, and Jones identified the rocket image to Duncan Sandys.[4][5][6]

events.title: The A-4 flies
events.text: After two failures the third A-4 rose from Test Stand VII at Peenemuende, flew 190 kilometres down the Baltic and reached about 85 kilometres' altitude. It was the first guided ballistic missile to work, and the first large rocket to fly the trajectory every launcher now flies: vertical climb, programmed pitch-over, burnout, ballistic coast. Walter Dornberger told his staff they had created the spaceship -- and then used it as artillery.

events.title: Mittelwerk: the rocket built by slave labour
events.text: After the RAF bombed Peenemuende, V-2 production was moved underground to the Mittelwerk tunnels in the Kohnstein, worked by prisoners from the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp. Around 60,000 prisoners passed through the camp system and roughly 20,000 died there -- of exhaustion, starvation, disease and execution. That is more people than the rocket killed when it was fired. This is not a footnote to the V-2's engineering; it is a condition of it, and the plant's operations director, Arthur Rudolph, later managed the Saturn V.

events.title: The first V-2 falls on a city
events.text: Two V-2s were fired at Paris and London on 8 September 1944; the London rocket destroyed houses in Chiswick and killed three people. There was no warning and no defence: the missile arrived faster than its own sound. About 3,000 were launched in anger before the launch sites were overrun, killing an estimated 9,000 civilians and military personnel, with Antwerp hit as heavily as London.

sources.title: Imperial War Museums, What was the V-2 rocket?

events.title: The first human-made object in space
events.text: A vertically launched test designated MW 18014 reached an altitude of about 176 kilometres -- well beyond the 100-kilometre Karman line now used as the boundary of space. It was the first object built by people to leave the atmosphere, and it was a weapons test. The same vehicle, flown on a ballistic trajectory three months later, was killing civilians in London and Antwerp.

events.title: Both sides take the rocket engineers home
events.text: Von Braun and about 120 of his staff surrendered to American troops and were brought to the United States under Operation Paperclip, with their wartime records quietly sanitised to get them past immigration rules; hundreds of V-2s and tonnes of drawings went with them. The Soviet Union captured the Mittelwerk site itself, and in Operation Osoaviakhim in October 1946 deported some 2,500 German specialists and their families eastward overnight. Both space programmes started from the same weapon.

events.title: The R-7 works, and changes the calculation
events.text: After three failures, Korolev's R-7 flew its full course to the Kamchatka peninsula on 21 August 1957 -- the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile. It was designed to carry a heavy, crude hydrogen bomb, which is why it had the lifting capacity to put something substantial in orbit. Four days after the Soviet announcement, Korolev had permission to launch a satellite with it.

events.title: Sputnik 1: the space age begins
events.text: An 83.6-kilogram polished sphere, pressurised with nitrogen and carrying two radio transmitters, reached orbit from Baikonur and began beeping on frequencies any amateur could receive. That was deliberate: the proof had to be public. It transmitted for 22 days, stayed up for three months, and converted spaceflight overnight from an enthusiasm into a matter of national standing. The original plan -- a sophisticated instrumented satellite -- was running late, so Korolev flew the simple sphere instead.

image.title: Первый в мире искусственный спутник Земли

events.title: Sputnik 2 carries Laika, and does not bring her back
events.text: A month after Sputnik 1, a half-tonne satellite carried a stray Moscow dog called Laika into orbit with no means of return -- the capsule had no re-entry system. She died within hours of overheating when the thermal control failed, a fact not admitted until 2002; the official account at the time described a planned euthanasia after a week. The flight proved a living animal could survive launch and weightlessness, and it is remembered as much for what it cost.

events.title: Vanguard fails on live television
events.text: The United States' chosen answer to Sputnik, a civilian Navy rocket carrying a 1.4-kilogram satellite, rose about a metre from its pad at Cape Canaveral, sank back and exploded in front of the assembled press. Newspapers called it Flopnik and Kaputnik. The failure handed the first American satellite to von Braun's Army team, who had been told to stand down a year earlier and had kept a rocket ready anyway.

events.title: Explorer 1 finds the radiation belts
events.text: America's first satellite weighed 14 kilograms and carried a Geiger counter built by James Van Allen. The counter saturated at certain altitudes and read almost nothing at others, which turned out to mean that Earth is wrapped in belts of charged particles trapped by its magnetic field. It was the first scientific discovery made in space -- and the first evidence that orbit is a hazardous environment, not merely an empty one.

events.title: NASA opens for business
events.text: The National Aeronautics and Space Act created a civilian space agency out of the old National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, with a statutory commitment to conduct its activities openly and share the results. That openness is the reason this page can be illustrated: almost everything NASA produces is in the public domain, which is why its photographs and drawings are everywhere and the Soviet equivalents are not.

events.title: Vanguard 1, the first solar-powered satellite
events.text: The fourth satellite ever launched was a 1.46-kilogram, 165-millimetre sphere with six antennas and the first solar cells flown on a spacecraft. Its radio worked for six years and its orbit, tracked for decades, revealed that Earth is very slightly pear-shaped. It is still up there: the oldest human-made object in orbit, and likely to remain so for centuries.

events.title: Luna 1 and 2 leave Earth's gravity
events.text: Luna 1 missed the Moon by about 6,000 kilometres in January 1959 and became the first object in orbit around the Sun, after venting a cloud of sodium gas bright enough to be photographed from the ground as proof. Luna 2, in September, hit the Moon -- the first human-made object to reach another world, scattering two engraved metal pennants on impact.

events.title: Luna 3 photographs the far side of the Moon
events.text: Luna 3 carried photographic film, developed it on board, scanned the negatives with a flying-spot scanner and radioed the results back through fading signal. Seventeen usable frames showed the hemisphere no one had ever seen: almost without the dark maria that dominate the near side, and heavily cratered. The Soviet Academy of Sciences named the features, which is why the far side has a Mare Moscoviense and a Tsiolkovsky crater.

events.title: The Chief Designer nobody could name
events.text: Soviet achievements were announced without names. Sputnik, Gagarin's flight and the Luna probes were credited to Soviet science and to an anonymous Chief Designer; Korolev was nominated for a Nobel Prize and the committee was told that the achievement belonged to the whole Soviet people. He was identified publicly only in his obituary in January 1966. The secrecy protected him from assassination and starved his programme of the political constituency that Apollo had.

events.title: Alan Shepard flies, 23 days later
events.text: Shepard's Mercury-Redstone flight was suborbital: fifteen minutes and 28 seconds, 187 kilometres high, down range into the Atlantic. He flew with manual control of attitude, which Gagarin had not, and he had waited on the pad long enough that he eventually asked the controllers to light the candle. It was a fortnight's worth of catching up, not a first, and everyone involved knew it.

events.title: Kennedy commits to a Moon landing before 1970
events.text: Twenty days after Shepard's flight, Kennedy asked Congress for a programme to land a man on the Moon and return him safely to the Earth before the decade was out. NASA had flown one person for fifteen minutes. The deadline was chosen because it was far enough away to be possible and near enough to be a race; it eventually consumed about four percent of the federal budget at its peak and employed some 400,000 people.

events.title: Yuri Gagarin orbits the Earth
events.text: Gagarin was launched from Baikonur in a 2.3-metre sphere, completed one orbit in 108 minutes and ejected to parachute separately into a field near Engels, where a farmer and her daughter met him. The spacecraft was flown automatically; nobody knew whether a person could think or swallow in weightlessness, so the manual controls were locked behind a combination. He was 27, and the first human being to see the whole Earth at once.

events.title: John Glenn orbits, with the numbers checked by hand
events.text: Glenn made three orbits in Friendship 7, flying part of the mission manually after the automatic attitude system drifted, and came home through a re-entry that controllers feared he might not survive -- a sensor suggested his heat shield had come loose. Before the flight he had asked that Katherine Johnson recompute the trajectory by hand, because he did not trust the new electronic computers that had produced it.

events.title: Mariner 2 flies past Venus
events.text: The first successful mission to another planet, after its twin failed at launch. Mariner 2 found no magnetic field, a surface hotter than 400 degrees Celsius and a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere -- demolishing the popular picture of a steamy, jungle-covered twin of Earth and making Venus the first example of a planet ruined by a runaway greenhouse effect.

events.title: Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space
events.text: A textile worker and amateur parachutist selected from 400 applicants, Tereshkova flew 48 orbits over three days aboard Vostok 6 -- more flight time than every American astronaut up to that point combined. No woman flew again for nineteen years, and no American woman until Sally Ride in 1983. She remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

events.title: Ranger, Surveyor and Lunar Orbiter map the ground
events.text: Apollo could not be planned on telescope views. Ranger 7 sent back 4,300 close-up pictures before crashing deliberately in 1964; five Surveyor craft soft-landed from 1966 and dug the soil to show it would bear weight; five Lunar Orbiters photographed 99 percent of the surface and chose the landing sites. Lunar Orbiter 1 also took the first picture of the Earth from the vicinity of the Moon, in August 1966.

events.title: Three in a capsule built for one
events.text: To stay ahead of the two-seat Gemini, Korolev's bureau stripped the ejection seat and some equipment out of a Vostok and fitted three couches. The crew flew without spacesuits because there was no room for them, and landed inside the capsule on a newly fitted retro-rocket system, since there was no longer any way to eject. It was a stunt, and the engineers said so afterwards.

events.title: Gemini 4 and the first American spacewalk
events.text: Ed White spent 21 minutes outside Gemini 4 manoeuvring with a hand-held gas gun and enjoying himself so much that getting him back in took an argument. The flight also tried to rendezvous with its spent booster and failed, teaching NASA the first lesson of orbital mechanics: to catch something ahead of you, you must slow down and drop to a lower, faster orbit.

image.title: Ed White First American Spacewalker - GPN-2000-001180

events.title: Two spacecraft meet in orbit
events.text: Gemini 6A flew to within 30 centimetres of Gemini 7 and the two held formation for more than five hours -- the first rendezvous, and the manoeuvre without which no lunar landing was possible. Gemini 7's crew stayed up for just under fourteen days in a cabin the size of the front seats of a small car, proving that a lunar round trip would not disable its crew.

events.title: Alexei Leonov walks in space, and nearly cannot get back
events.text: Leonov left Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock for twelve minutes outside. His suit ballooned in vacuum until his hands pulled out of the gloves and he could not fit through the hatch; he bled the suit's pressure down below safe limits and forced his way in head first, soaked in sweat. The automatic re-entry then failed and the crew landed in deep snow in the Urals, waiting two nights for rescue.
