image.credit: Soviet Space Program, traced to SVG by C records

events.title: Mariner 4 photographs Mars
events.text: Twenty-one pictures, taken in a few minutes from 9,800 kilometres and returned over eight hours at 8.3 bits per second, showed a cratered, cold, almost airless surface. The impatient team at JPL hand-coloured a printout of the first numerical data with pastels before the image processing finished. A century of speculation about canals and vegetation ended that afternoon.

events.title: The first docking, and the first emergency
events.text: Neil Armstrong and David Scott docked Gemini 8 with an unmanned Agena target -- the first joining of two spacecraft in orbit. Half an hour later a stuck thruster set the combination spinning at one revolution per second, close to the point where the crew would have blacked out. Armstrong undocked, shut down the manoeuvring system and used the re-entry thrusters to stop the roll, which forced an immediate landing in the Pacific.

events.title: Luna 9 lands softly, and sends a panorama
events.text: An airbag-cushioned capsule, ejected before touchdown and left to bounce to a stop in Oceanus Procellarum, opened four petals and transmitted the first pictures taken from the surface of another world. They settled a real argument: the lunar soil was firm, not a deep dust layer that would swallow a spacecraft. The images were intercepted and published by Jodrell Bank in England before the Soviet Union released them.

events.title: The Apollo 1 fire
events.text: During a ground test with the cabin sealed and pressurised with pure oxygen above atmospheric pressure, a spark somewhere in the wiring started a fire that killed Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee in seconds. The hatch opened inward and could not be removed in time. The programme stopped for twenty months; the command module was rebuilt with a quick-release outward hatch, a mixed-gas cabin atmosphere at launch and non-flammable materials. Apollo almost certainly reached the Moon because of what the fire forced.

events.title: The Saturn V flies, all stages live, first time
events.text: George Mueller's all-up testing doctrine said that every stage of the Saturn V would be live and real on its first flight, instead of being tested one at a time. Von Braun's engineers thought this reckless. Apollo 4 worked: 2,800 tonnes of rocket lifted off, all three stages performed, and the command module was flung back into the atmosphere at lunar return speed to prove the heat shield. The decision probably saved two years.

events.title: Soyuz 1 kills Vladimir Komarov
events.text: The first Soyuz was flown before it was ready, sixteen months after Korolev's death and under political pressure for an anniversary. One solar panel failed to deploy, the attitude control misbehaved, the planned second launch and docking was cancelled, and on re-entry the main parachute would not leave its container. Komarov died on impact -- the first person to die during a spaceflight. The design was fixed and flew for the next sixty years.

events.title: Apollo 8 leaves Earth orbit
events.text: With the lunar module running late, George Low proposed in August 1968 that the next flight go round the Moon without one. Four months later Borman, Lovell and Anders became the first people to leave Earth's gravitational influence, to see the far side with their own eyes, and to watch the Earth rise over the lunar horizon -- Anders's photograph of it is probably the most reproduced image ever taken in space.

events.title: Apollo 11 lands
events.text: Armstrong and Aldrin landed Eagle in the Sea of Tranquillity with about 25 seconds of hovering fuel left, after taking manual control to avoid a boulder field and after the guidance computer threw a series of 1202 alarms that Margaret Hamilton's software was able to shed and recover from. They spent two and a half hours outside. An estimated 600 million people -- a fifth of the world -- watched or listened.

image.title: A Man on the Moon, AS11-40-5903 (cropped)

events.title: Apollo 12 proves it can be done on purpose
events.text: Struck by lightning twice during launch and saved by a flight controller who remembered an obscure switch, Apollo 12 then landed within 160 metres of the Surveyor 3 probe that had been sitting on the Moon for two and a half years. Pinpoint landing mattered more than it sounds: it turned the Moon from somewhere you could reach into somewhere you could choose to go.

events.title: The N1 fails four times
events.text: The Soviet Moon rocket had thirty engines in its first stage and no facility to test the assembled stage on the ground -- the money had gone elsewhere. The first launch in February 1969 failed at 68 seconds; the second, in July 1969, fell back and destroyed its launch complex; two more attempts failed in 1971 and 1972. The programme was suspended in 1974 and cancelled in 1976, and the Soviet Union denied having had a lunar programme at all until 1989.

image.title: N1 1M1 mockup on the launch pad at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in late 1967

events.title: Apollo 13 comes home on the lunar module
events.text: Two days out, an oxygen tank in the service module exploded, crippling the command module's power and water. The crew shut it down and moved into the lunar module, which was designed for two men for two days and kept three alive for four, swinging round the Moon and back while controllers improvised a carbon-dioxide scrubber from parts aboard and wrote a power-up procedure from nothing. The landing was lost; everybody survived.

events.title: Luna 16 brings back a sample without a crew
events.text: Two months after Apollo 13, a Soviet robot landed in Mare Fecunditatis, drilled 35 centimetres into the soil, sealed 101 grams in a capsule and flew it back to Kazakhstan. It was the first automated sample return from another world and the answer to a question that is still live: how much of what a crew does can be done by machine, and for how much less.

events.title: Lunokhod 1 drives on the Moon
events.text: The first rover on another world was a sealed bathtub on eight independently driven wire-mesh wheels, warmed through the fourteen-day lunar night by a polonium heater and steered from Earth by a five-person crew watching low-rate television with a two-second delay. It covered 10.5 kilometres in ten lunar days. Its successor, Lunokhod 2, drove 39 kilometres in 1973 -- a distance no rover beat for forty years.

events.title: The Venera landers survive Venus, briefly
events.text: Venera 7 transmitted for 23 minutes from the surface in December 1970 -- the first signal from the surface of another planet -- measuring 475 degrees Celsius and 90 atmospheres. Venera 9 sent the first picture in 1975, and Venera 13 lasted 127 minutes in 1982 and returned colour panoramas of flat orange rock. No spacecraft has operated on Venus since, and nothing has lasted more than two hours.

events.title: Mariner 9 orbits Mars into a global dust storm
events.text: The first spacecraft to orbit another planet arrived to find Mars entirely hidden by dust. Controllers waited. When the air cleared, the pictures showed the volcanoes of Tharsis, the 4,000-kilometre canyon system now called Valles Marineris and dry river channels -- a planet with a violent geological history, not the dead cratered ball Mariner 4's narrow strip had suggested.

events.title: Salyut 1, the first space station
events.text: Nineteen tonnes of pressurised laboratory launched on a Proton, with a docking port for Soyuz ferries. The first crew, Soyuz 10, could not get a hard dock and came home. The second, Soyuz 11, lived aboard for 23 days. The station was deliberately destroyed in October 1971, after a programme that had been approved partly to give Soviet crewed spaceflight a purpose once the Moon was lost.

events.title: The Soyuz 11 crew dies on the way home
events.text: Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov and Viktor Patsayev undocked from Salyut 1 after 23 days and were found dead in their seats after an apparently perfect landing. A pressure-equalisation valve had jolted open at module separation, 168 kilometres up, and the cabin lost its air in under two minutes. They were not wearing pressure suits, because the three-seat cabin had no room for them. Soyuz was rebuilt for two suited crew, and nobody has flown a re-entry without a suit since.

image.title: The Soviet Union 1971 CPA 4060 stamp (Cosmonauts Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov and Viktor Patsayev)

events.title: The last three landings carry a car and a geologist
events.text: Apollo 15, 16 and 17 were the science missions: a battery-powered rover extended each crew's range from a few hundred metres to several kilometres, stays grew to three days, and Apollo 17 carried Harrison Schmitt, a professional geologist. On 14 December 1972 Eugene Cernan climbed the ladder for the last time. Apollo 18, 19 and 20 had already been cancelled; their Saturn Vs are in museums.

image.title: Eugene Cernan at the LM, Apollo 17, AS17-134-20378

events.title: Pioneer 10 and 11 cross the asteroid belt to Jupiter
events.text: Nobody knew whether a spacecraft could survive the asteroid belt or Jupiter's radiation; the Pioneers were sent to find out, and both got through. Pioneer 10 passed Jupiter in December 1973 and Pioneer 11 went on to make the first flyby of Saturn in 1979. Each carries a gold-anodised plaque showing a man and a woman and the Sun's position relative to fourteen pulsars.

image.title: An artist's impression of a Pioneer spacecraft on its way to interstellar space

events.title: Skylab is launched broken and repaired in orbit
events.text: A converted Saturn V third stage with 351 cubic metres of room -- more than the ISS gives any single crew today. During launch the meteoroid and sun shield tore away, taking one solar wing with it and jamming the other; the workshop heated towards 80 degrees. The first crew flew up with an improvised parasol, deployed it through a scientific airlock, and then freed the stuck wing by hand on a spacewalk. Three crews stayed 28, 59 and 84 days.

events.title: Apollo and Soyuz dock
events.text: An American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz joined in orbit using a purpose-built androgynous docking adapter that also bridged the two spacecraft's different cabin pressures and atmospheres. Thomas Stafford and Alexei Leonov shook hands through the hatch. It was the last flight of an Apollo command module, the first international crewed docking, and the ancestor of the docking standards that let Dragon and Soyuz use the same ports today.

events.title: Viking lands on Mars and looks for life
events.text: Seven years to the day after Apollo 11, Viking 1's lander touched down in Chryse Planitia; Viking 2 followed in September. Between them they operated for six and four years, photographed the surface in colour and ran three biology experiments. One returned a positive result that nobody has been able to reproduce or explain away as chemistry alone, which is why the Viking biology data is still argued about fifty years later.

events.title: Salyut 6 and 7 make long duration routine
events.text: Two docking ports instead of one changed everything: a station could be resupplied by uncrewed Progress freighters while a crew was aboard, and visited by a second Soyuz. Crews stayed for 96, then 140, then 185, then 237 days. Guest cosmonauts from Czechoslovakia, Poland, East Germany, Cuba, Mongolia, Vietnam, France and India flew under the Interkosmos programme -- the first people in space from outside the two superpowers.

events.title: The Voyagers leave, carrying a record
events.text: Two spacecraft launched a fortnight apart to exploit an alignment of the outer planets that recurs every 175 years. Each carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record holding 115 images, greetings in 55 languages, natural sounds and ninety minutes of music from Bach to Blind Willie Johnson, with instructions for playing it etched on the cover -- assembled by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan in six weeks.

events.title: Columbia flies the first Space Shuttle mission
events.text: Twenty years to the day after Gagarin, John Young and Robert Crippen rode the first Space Shuttle to orbit -- the first crewed spacecraft flown with people aboard on its maiden flight, with solid boosters that could not be shut down and no escape system after the first two minutes. It worked. The promise was airline-like operations at a fraction of expendable cost; the reality was never close, but the vehicle could do things nothing else could.

events.title: Challenger breaks up after launch, killing seven
events.text: A rubber O-ring in a solid booster joint, stiff in the morning's unprecedented cold, failed to seal; hot gas cut into the external tank and the stack came apart 73 seconds after liftoff. Francis Scobee, Michael Smith, Judith Resnik, Ronald McNair, Ellison Onizuka, Gregory Jarvis and Christa McAuliffe died. Engineers at the booster contractor had argued against launching that morning and been overruled. The Rogers Commission found an organisation that had come to treat a known flaw as an acceptable risk.

events.title: Mir's core module reaches orbit
events.text: Mir was the first modular station: a core with six docking ports, to which six more modules were added over the next decade. It was occupied almost continuously for twelve and a half years, survived an onboard fire and a collision with a Progress freighter, and taught the world most of what it knows about keeping people healthy in orbit for a year at a time. Valeri Polyakov spent 437 continuous days aboard in 1994 and 1995 -- still the record.

image.title: Mir Space Station viewed from Endeavour during STS-89

events.title: Buran flies once, automatically, and is never flown again
events.text: The Soviet shuttle launched on Energia, orbited twice and landed itself on a runway at Baikonur in a crosswind, with nobody aboard -- an automatic landing the American orbiter was never built to perform. It was the only flight. The Soviet Union dissolved three years later, and the single flown orbiter was destroyed in 2002 when the roof of its hangar collapsed.

events.title: The grand tour: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
events.text: Between them the Voyagers found volcanoes on Io, a possible ocean under Europa's ice, Saturn's braided rings and Titan's thick atmosphere, then Voyager 2 alone went on to Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989 -- the only visits either planet has ever had. At Neptune it flew 4,950 kilometres above the cloud tops and found nitrogen geysers on Triton. No spacecraft has been sent to either planet since.

events.title: Hubble is launched with the wrong mirror, and repaired
events.text: The telescope's 2.4-metre primary mirror had been ground to the wrong figure by about two microns, blurring every image. Because Hubble was designed to be serviced by the Shuttle, a 1993 mission fitted corrective optics and the observatory became the most productive telescope ever built. Four further servicing missions replaced its instruments, gyroscopes and solar arrays; it is still working thirty-six years on.

events.title: Galileo orbits Jupiter and drops a probe into it
events.text: Galileo's main antenna jammed half-open, so fourteen years of data came home through a low-gain antenna at a few hundred bits per second, with heroic data compression. It still delivered: a probe that transmitted for 58 minutes as it fell through Jupiter's atmosphere, and the magnetic evidence for a salty ocean beneath Europa's ice that Europa Clipper is now going to examine.

events.title: A Shuttle docks with Mir
events.text: Atlantis docked with Mir using an adapter descended from the Apollo-Soyuz hardware, beginning three years of joint flights in which seven American astronauts lived aboard the Russian station. The Shuttle-Mir programme was partly diplomacy and partly a rehearsal: NASA had never operated a station long-term, Russia had done little else, and the International Space Station needed both.

events.title: Mars Pathfinder bounces to a stop and lets a rover out
events.text: Pathfinder landed by airbag -- no retro-rockets at touchdown, just a bounce across the rocks of Ares Vallis -- and released Sojourner, an 11-kilogram rover the size of a microwave oven. It was built fast and cheap as a deliberate test of whether that was possible after the billion-dollar Vikings, and its website was one of the first global internet events.

events.title: The first ISS module is launched
events.text: Zarya, a Russian-built and American-funded control module descended from Chelomei's TKS design, went up on a Proton; two weeks later the Shuttle brought the American Unity node and bolted the two together. Over the next thirteen years more than forty flights assembled the rest. The station was built in pieces that had never been mated on the ground, by two countries that had spent thirty years pointing missiles at each other.

events.title: People move in, and never leave
events.text: William Shepherd, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev arrived on a Soyuz and opened up the station. It has been occupied continuously ever since -- more than a quarter of a century at the time of writing, the longest unbroken human presence off Earth. Every person born since 2 November 2000 has lived their whole life with people in space.

events.title: Mir is brought down over the Pacific
events.text: After fifteen years, with Russia unable to fund two stations at once, Mir was deliberately deorbited: a Progress freighter fired its engines to drop the 130-tonne complex into the atmosphere over the South Pacific, east of New Zealand. Most of it burned; the heaviest fragments fell into the ocean. It remains the largest object ever deliberately brought down from orbit -- a record the ISS is scheduled to take in 2031.

image.title: Mir Space Station viewed from Endeavour during STS-89

events.title: Columbia breaks up on re-entry, killing seven
events.text: A piece of insulating foam from the external tank had struck the leading edge of Columbia's left wing at launch, punching a hole in the heat shield that nobody on the ground was able to assess. Sixteen days later the wing failed during re-entry over Texas. Rick Husband, William McCool, Michael Anderson, David Brown, Kalpana Chawla, Laurel Clark and Ilan Ramon died. The accident board found the same organisational pattern as Challenger: a recurring anomaly reclassified as normal.

events.title: Cassini-Huygens at Saturn
events.text: Thirteen years in orbit: water-ice geysers erupting from Enceladus's south pole, lakes of liquid methane on Titan, new moons and the structure of the rings. ESA's Huygens probe parachuted onto Titan in January 2005, the only landing ever made in the outer Solar System. With fuel running out, Cassini was deliberately flown into Saturn in 2017 so that it could never crash into a moon that might be habitable.

events.title: Spirit and Opportunity, sent for ninety days
events.text: Two solar-powered rovers landed three weeks apart with a design life of 90 Martian days. Spirit worked for six years before getting stuck in soft sand; Opportunity drove 45 kilometres over fourteen years and found the layered sulphates and iron spherules that showed water had once stood on the surface. Its last message, during a planet-wide dust storm in 2018, reported falling power and darkening skies.

events.title: The Shuttle flies for the last time
events.text: Atlantis landed at Kennedy Space Center at the end of STS-135, closing a thirty-year programme of 135 missions that built the ISS, launched and repaired Hubble, and killed fourteen people. It left the United States without a way to launch its own astronauts for nine years; every American crew between 2011 and 2020 flew on a Russian Soyuz, at a price that rose to over 80 million dollars a seat.

events.title: Curiosity is lowered onto Mars by a rocket crane
events.text: A 900-kilogram nuclear-powered laboratory was too heavy for airbags, so it was flown down on a hovering descent stage and winched to the surface on three cables -- a sequence of events that had never been tested end to end and could not be. It worked first time. Curiosity found the chemistry of an ancient freshwater lake within its first year and has been climbing a mountain of sediment ever since.

image.title: Curiosity Self-Portrait at 'Big Sky' Drilling Site

events.title: The Voyagers reach interstellar space
events.text: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause -- the boundary where the Sun's wind gives way to the interstellar medium -- in August 2012, and Voyager 2 followed in November 2018, giving two measurements of a boundary nobody had sampled before. Both still transmit on a few watts. Instruments are being switched off one by one to stretch the plutonium out; the last ones are expected to go silent in the 2030s.

sources.title: NASA, Where Are Voyager 1 and 2 Now?

events.title: Philae lands on a comet
events.text: After a ten-year chase including three Earth flybys and 31 months in hibernation, ESA's Rosetta reached comet 67P and released the washing-machine-sized Philae. Its anchoring harpoons failed, so it bounced twice over two hours and came to rest in a shadowed crack, where it worked for 60 hours on primary batteries before the cold took it. Rosetta followed the comet through its closest approach to the Sun and then landed on it too.

events.title: An orbital rocket lands on its tail
events.text: After several failures at sea, a Falcon 9 first stage returned to Cape Canaveral and set itself down upright on a concrete pad, nine minutes after launching eleven satellites. The physics had never been in doubt; doing it with enough margin, accuracy and reliability to be worth the lost payload was the hard part. It is the single change that has done most to reduce the cost of reaching orbit.

events.title: New Horizons flies past Pluto
events.text: After nine and a half years and five billion kilometres, a spacecraft the size of a grand piano swept 12,500 kilometres above Pluto at 14 kilometres a second, with one chance and no possibility of a correction. The data took sixteen months to trickle home. It showed nitrogen-ice glaciers flowing on a world at minus 230 degrees, mountains of water ice, and no craters on the brightest plains -- a geologically active body at the edge of the Solar System.

image.credit: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), Applied Physics Laboratory

events.title: A used booster flies again
events.text: Landing a rocket proves nothing on its own; flying the same one again is the point. The booster that had delivered cargo to the ISS in April 2016 launched the SES-10 communications satellite eleven months later and landed again. By August 2026 a single Falcon 9 first stage had flown 37 times, approaching the 39 missions flown by the most-used Space Shuttle orbiter.

image.title: SES-10 Launch - world's first reflight of an orbital class rocket (33361035200)

sources.title: Wikipedia, List of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launches

events.title: Falcon Heavy's first flight, with two boosters landing together
events.text: Twenty-seven engines lit at once, and the two side boosters came back to adjacent landing pads and touched down in near-synchrony. The test payload was a used Tesla car with a mannequin in a spacesuit, which embarrassed some observers and was watched by several million people. Falcon Heavy has since launched the Psyche asteroid mission and Europa Clipper.

events.title: Chang'e 4 lands on the far side of the Moon
events.text: The far side never faces Earth, so a lander there cannot be spoken to directly. China first placed the Queqiao relay satellite in a halo orbit beyond the Moon, then set Chang'e 4 down in Von Karman crater inside the South Pole-Aitken basin and drove the Yutu-2 rover out. It was the first landing on the far side by anyone, and Yutu-2 is still the longest-lived lunar rover.

events.title: Crew Dragon carries astronauts, the first commercial crewed flight
events.text: Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken flew to the ISS in a capsule built and operated by a private company under a fixed-price NASA contract -- the first crewed orbital flight by a vehicle not owned by a government, and the first American crew launch since 2011. Crew Dragon has flown routinely since, and in 2024 it brought home the two astronauts whose Starliner could not safely carry them.

events.title: Hayabusa and Hayabusa2 bring back pieces of asteroids
events.text: The first Hayabusa limped home in 2010 with a few micrograms of Itokawa dust after a catalogue of failures that should have ended the mission. Its successor did the job properly: Hayabusa2 fired a copper slug into Ryugu to expose fresh material, landed twice, and parachuted 5.4 grams into the Australian desert in December 2020. The samples contain amino acids and water-bearing minerals older than the Earth.

events.title: The first orbital flight with no professional astronaut aboard
events.text: Inspiration4 put four private citizens -- a billionaire pilot, a childhood cancer survivor working as a physician assistant, a data engineer and a geoscientist -- into a three-day free-flying orbit with nobody aboard who had flown before. It raised money for a children's hospital, and it marked the point at which orbital spaceflight stopped being something only state employees did.

image.title: Inspiration4 Launch (210915-F-CG053-1004)
image.credit: U.S. Space Force Photo by Staff Sgt. JT Armstrong

events.title: Webb launches, unfolds, and sees further than Hubble
events.text: The James Webb Space Telescope launched folded inside an Ariane 5 and spent two weeks deploying a 6.5-metre segmented mirror and a tennis-court-sized sunshield, through 344 single-point failures with no possibility of repair a million and a half kilometres away. Every step worked, and Ariane's accuracy left enough fuel for roughly twenty years of operation. Its first images, in July 2022, showed galaxies from the first few hundred million years of the universe.

events.title: Perseverance lands, and a helicopter flies on Mars
events.text: Perseverance touched down in Jezero crater, an ancient river delta, to collect rock cores for an eventual return to Earth. Strapped to its belly was Ingenuity, a 1.8-kilogram helicopter sent to test whether powered flight was possible in air one percent as dense as ours. It was meant to fly five times in a month; it flew 72 times over nearly three years before damaging a rotor blade.

events.title: Artemis I flies an empty Orion around the Moon
events.text: The first flight of the Space Launch System sent an uncrewed Orion 430,000 kilometres from Earth, further than any crew-rated spacecraft had been, and brought it home through a lunar-return re-entry at 40,000 kilometres an hour. The rocket worked on its first attempt after years of delay and a cost that NASA's own inspector general has called unsustainable.

image.title: Orion Approaches Moon for Outbound Powered Flyby

events.title: Tiangong is completed
events.text: China assembled its own station in nineteen months: the Tianhe core module in April 2021, the Wentian and Mengtian laboratories in 2022, and a permanent crew from June 2022. Excluded from the ISS by American law since 2011, China built an alternative at about a fifth of the ISS's mass, and has kept it crewed by Shenzhou rotations ever since. There are now two inhabited space stations.

events.title: Chandrayaan-3 lands near the lunar south pole
events.text: Four years after Chandrayaan-2's lander crashed, ISRO's Vikram touched down at about 69 degrees south -- further towards a pole than any spacecraft before it -- and released the 26-kilogram Pragyan rover for one lunar day. India became the fourth country to land on the Moon, on a mission whose total cost was reported as less than many feature films.

events.title: OSIRIS-REx delivers 121 grams of asteroid Bennu
events.text: The spacecraft touched Bennu for about five seconds, blew nitrogen into the surface to stir up loose material, and caught so much of it that the sampler head would not close properly. The capsule landed in the Utah desert with 121.6 grams -- the largest sample ever returned from beyond the Moon, carrying carbon compounds and clay minerals from the formation of the Solar System. The spacecraft flew on towards the asteroid Apophis.

image.title: OSIRIS-REx spacecraft model
image.credit: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) / Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) / University of Arizona / Lockheed Martin

events.title: Starship's first integrated flight ends in a deliberate explosion
events.text: The largest rocket ever built cleared the pad, lost several engines, failed to separate its stages, tumbled and was destroyed by its own flight-termination system four minutes in. It also blew a crater under the launch mount and scattered concrete for hundreds of metres. SpaceX called it a success on the grounds that the data was the product; regulators and ecologists took a different view, and the next flight was eight months later.

events.title: Chang'e 6 returns the first far-side samples
events.text: Launched on 3 May 2024, Chang'e 6 scooped and drilled 1,935.3 grams of material from the South Pole-Aitken basin -- the oldest and deepest impact structure on the Moon -- and landed it in Inner Mongolia on 25 June. Every previous lunar sample, American or Soviet, came from the near side. The far-side material is chemically different, and is being used to work out why the Moon's two hemispheres are not alike.

sources.title: CNSA, Chang'e-6 collects 1,935.3 grams of samples from the Moon's far side

events.title: Europa Clipper sets out for Jupiter's ocean moon
events.text: The largest spacecraft NASA has built for a planetary mission launched on a Falcon Heavy to answer one question: could the salt-water ocean under Europa's ice support life? It flew past Mars for a gravity assist in March 2025, passes Earth in December 2026, and arrives at Jupiter in 2030 for nearly fifty close passes of the moon. Dragonfly, a nuclear-powered rotorcraft for Titan, is scheduled to follow in July 2028.
events.vintage: Mission timeline as published by NASA and checked on 10 October 2026.

image.credit: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) · Jet Propulsion Laboratory

events.title: The ISS gets an end date
events.text: In June 2024 NASA awarded SpaceX a contract worth up to 843 million dollars to build a US Deorbit Vehicle -- a Dragon with an enlarged trunk full of engines -- to bring the station down safely. Operations are funded to the end of 2030 and the controlled deorbit into a remote stretch of ocean is planned for January 2031. Nothing that large has ever been brought down deliberately; commercial stations are meant to replace it, and none has yet flown.
events.vintage: Checked against NASA's own pages on 10 October 2026; the 2031 deorbit is a plan.

events.title: Starliner's crewed test flight goes wrong
events.text: Boeing's capsule reached the ISS with Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams aboard, but five of its eight approach thrusters misbehaved and helium leaked from the service module. NASA decided a crewed return was too risky; Starliner came home empty in September 2024 and its crew stayed on the station until a Crew Dragon brought them back. In February 2026 the flight was reclassified as a Type A mishap, NASA's most serious category.

image.title: NASA’s Boeing Crew Flight Test Launch (NHQ202406050029)

events.title: The launch tower catches the booster
events.text: On Starship's fifth test flight the 71-metre Super Heavy booster flew back to its own launch tower and was caught in mid-air by two steel arms, seven minutes after liftoff. Removing the landing legs and the sea platform from a reusable booster is only worth attempting if the guidance is good to within centimetres; it was. The catch has since been repeated.

image.title: Starship Booster Return on Final Approach (54063904149)

events.title: A commercial lander succeeds on the Moon
events.text: Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost landed upright in Mare Crisium and completed a full two-week mission with NASA instruments aboard -- the first fully successful landing under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme, which buys delivery rather than building the spacecraft. The two attempts before it, Intuitive Machines' IM-1 in 2024 and IM-2 in 2025, both reached the surface and tipped over.
events.vintage: Checked against live sources on 10 October 2026.

image.title: Blue Ghost M1 on the Moon

events.title: Blue Origin's New Glenn reaches orbit, then lands, then stumbles
events.text: New Glenn's first flight in January 2025 reached orbit but lost its booster. On the second, in November 2025, the booster landed on a ship at sea -- the second company ever to recover an orbital first stage. The third, in April 2026, re-flew and landed that booster but left its satellite in a useless orbit after an upper-stage fault. A static-fire explosion in May 2026 then damaged the launch complex badly enough to put the schedule in doubt.
events.vintage: Checked against live sources on 10 October 2026; these events postdate the compiler's own knowledge.

image.title: New Glenn - BlueBird 7 Launch (9628277) (cropped)
image.credit: U.S. Space Force photo by Gwendolyn Kurzen

sources.title: Wikipedia, List of New Glenn launches

events.title: Artemis II carries four people round the Moon
events.text: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and the Canadian Space Agency's Jeremy Hansen launched on 1 April 2026 for a ten-day free-return flight around the Moon -- the first crewed lunar mission since Apollo 17 in 1972. They travelled 252,756 miles from Earth, a record distance for a crewed spacecraft, saw parts of the far side that no human eyes had seen, and splashed down in the Pacific on 10 April.
events.vintage: Checked against NASA's own mission pages on 10 October 2026; this event postdates the compiler's own knowledge.

sources.title: NASA, Liftoff! NASA Launches Astronauts on Historic Artemis Moon Mission

events.title: The next landing slips: Artemis III becomes a rehearsal
events.text: With neither lunar lander ready, NASA restructured the programme in February 2026: Artemis III, planned as the first landing, becomes a crewed demonstration in Earth orbit in which Orion docks in turn with a Blue Origin Blue Moon test article and a SpaceX Starship pathfinder. The first crewed landing since 1972 moves to Artemis IV, currently targeted for 2028. Dates in this part of the timeline have moved before and may move again.
events.vintage: Status as checked on 10 October 2026; schedules beyond that date are plans, not facts.

events.title: China builds towards a crewed landing by 2030
events.text: The hardware for a Chinese Moon landing is in test: the Long March 10 rocket, the Mengzhou crew spacecraft and the Lanyue lander have completed static fires, pad-abort and landing-and-takeoff tests, with an uncrewed Mengzhou orbital flight expected late in 2026. Meanwhile Shenzhou 23, launched on 24 May 2026, took three crew to Tiangong including the first astronaut from Hong Kong and a planned year-long stay in orbit. The stated target for a crewed landing is 2030.
events.vintage: Checked against live sources on 10 October 2026; the 2030 landing target is China's stated plan, not an accomplished fact.

events.title: India prepares to launch its own astronauts
events.text: ISRO's Gaganyaan programme has completed pad-abort and crew-module qualification tests and plans three uncrewed flights before a crewed mission; the first, carrying a half-humanoid robot called Vyommitra, is scheduled for late 2026, with a crewed flight targeted for 2027. If it flies, India becomes the fourth country to launch people on its own vehicle, after the Soviet Union, the United States and China.
events.vintage: Status as checked on 10 October 2026; these are scheduled flights, not completed ones.

events.title: Starship reaches orbit
events.text: The fourteenth test flight put Starship into orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink satellites -- the first Starship mission to carry a paying payload. Two booster engines and one on the ship misbehaved, and the flight was cut short at its first checkpoint, returning to a Pacific splashdown about seven hours earlier than planned. Both primary objectives, orbit and deployment, were met.
events.vintage: Checked against live sources on 10 October 2026; this event postdates the compiler's own knowledge.

sources.title: SpaceX, Starship's Thirteenth Flight Test (mission log)

events.title: The Voyagers start switching themselves off
events.text: Both spacecraft lose about four watts a year as their plutonium decays. Engineers turned off Voyager 1's cosmic-ray subsystem in February 2025 and Voyager 2's low-energy charged-particle instrument in March 2025, then Voyager 1's low-energy charged-particle experiment in April 2026, with Voyager 2's cosmic-ray detector due to follow. Each spacecraft keeps a magnetometer and a plasma-wave instrument running -- the last measurements anyone will have from inside the interstellar medium for decades.
events.vintage: Checked against NASA and JPL mission updates on 10 October 2026.

cutaways.title: Saturn V, stage by stage
cutaways.note: The drawing carries the artist's own numbered arrows and lettered stage divisions with their lengths printed on it. We have not guessed at what the thirteen numbers mean; our legend reads the four lettered divisions, whose printed lengths match the published stage dimensions.

callouts.label: S-IC first stage, 42 m
callouts.note: Five F-1 engines burning kerosene and liquid oxygen for two and a half minutes, consuming about 2,000 tonnes of propellant.

callouts.label: S-II second stage, 24.8 m
callouts.note: Five J-2 engines on liquid hydrogen and oxygen, with the two tanks sharing a single insulated bulkhead to save weight.

callouts.label: S-IVB third stage and instrument unit, 19 m
callouts.note: One restartable J-2: it fires once to reach orbit and again, an orbit or two later, to send the spacecraft to the Moon.

callouts.label: Apollo spacecraft and escape tower, 24.7 m
callouts.note: The command and service modules, the lunar module folded inside its adapter, and the solid-fuelled escape tower that would pull the crew clear of a failing rocket.

cutaways.title: Apollo command and service module
cutaways.note: A NASA engineering drawing from the Apollo 10 era, labelled at source. Our numbered points sit beside those labels and explain what the parts meant for the mission rather than repeating their names.

callouts.label: The command module, 3.9 m across
callouts.note: The only part of the 110-metre stack that came home: a cone with an ablative heat shield, 5.9 cubic metres of living space for three people, and twelve days of endurance.

callouts.label: The crew access hatch
callouts.note: Redesigned after the Apollo 1 fire to open outward and unlatch in seconds; the original inward-opening hatch could not be removed in time to save Grissom, White and Chaffee.

callouts.label: Three foldable crew couches
callouts.note: Max Faget's layout. The couches folded away to free the floor, which is how three adults lived in a volume smaller than a small car's interior.

callouts.label: Ablative heat shield
callouts.note: An epoxy resin in a honeycomb matrix that is designed to char and flake away, carrying the heat of a 40,000 km/h lunar return with it.

callouts.label: Service propulsion engine
callouts.note: A single 91-kilonewton engine with no backup. It had to work to leave lunar orbit; Apollo's crews called the moment of that burn, on the far side and out of radio contact, the longest wait of the flight.

callouts.label: Service module sectors
callouts.note: Propellant, oxygen, hydrogen and fuel cells packed around a central tunnel. It was an oxygen tank in one of these sectors that exploded on Apollo 13.

image.title: Cutaway view of the Apollo 10 spacecraft (S69-34072)

sources.title: Wikipedia, Apollo command and service module

cutaways.title: Apollo Lunar Module
cutaways.note: NASA Marshall's own lunar-module diagram, labelled at source. The two stages are the whole idea: the descent stage, with the throttleable engine and the landing gear, is left behind on the Moon and serves as the launch pad for the ascent stage.

cutaways.title: Space Shuttle orbiter
cutaways.note: A NASA cutaway illustration, labelled at source. Our points mark the four features that made the orbiter unlike anything before or since -- and the two that made it dangerous.

callouts.label: Payload bay, 18.3 by 4.6 metres
callouts.note: Big enough for a bus, and the only cargo hold that ever came back down: satellites could be launched, retrieved, repaired and returned.

callouts.label: The manipulator arm
callouts.note: Canada's 15-metre robot arm, used to deploy satellites, to berth modules during ISS assembly and -- after Columbia -- to inspect the orbiter's own heat shield in orbit.

callouts.label: Flight deck and mid-deck
callouts.note: Up to seven crew, in two decks, with no escape system usable above about 30 kilometres.

callouts.label: Three RS-25 main engines
callouts.note: The most efficient engines ever flown on a first stage, fed from the external tank -- and recovered and reused with the orbiter. Four of them fly on each Space Launch System core today, expended.

callouts.label: Delta wing and elevons
callouts.note: The wings were there for a runway landing and for cross-range after a single-orbit military mission; they also added mass and the fragile leading-edge panels that Columbia lost.

callouts.label: Body flap and thermal tiles
callouts.note: About 24,000 individually shaped silica tiles, each in its own numbered place. A single breach in this surface is what destroyed Columbia in 2003.

cutaways.title: Skylab orbital workshop
cutaways.note: A 1973 Marshall Space Flight Center cutaway of the converted Saturn V third stage, labelled at source. Our points pick out what it was like to live in 351 cubic metres -- more room than any station crew has had since.

callouts.label: Entry hatch and airlock
callouts.note: The only way in, from the docked Apollo command module above. It was also the way out: the first crew went through it to free the jammed solar wing.

callouts.label: The grid floor
callouts.note: A triangular metal lattice through the crew deck. Astronauts wore cleated shoes that twisted into the holes, which is how you stand still in weightlessness.

callouts.label: The shower
callouts.note: A collapsible cylinder with a hand-held sprayer and a vacuum to suck the water back. It worked, took most of an hour to use, and was not repeated on later stations.

callouts.label: The lower tank, repurposed
callouts.note: Skylab was a Saturn V third stage: this dome was the liquid-hydrogen tank, and in orbit it became the waste tank.

callouts.label: Lockers and film vaults
callouts.note: The solar telescope shot photographic film, which had to be retrieved by spacewalk and brought home in the capsule -- there was no other way to return the data.

image.title: Cutaway View of Skylab Orbital Workshop 0101589

cutaways.title: Mercury capsule
cutaways.note: A NASA cutaway illustration with no labels of its own, so every point here is ours. The capsule is drawn with its blunt heat-shield end to the left -- the end that faces forward during re-entry.

callouts.label: Heat shield and retro-pack
callouts.note: The wide blunt end. Faget's insight was that a blunt body pushes its shock wave ahead of it and keeps most of the heat out of the structure; three retro-rockets strapped across it slowed the capsule for re-entry.

callouts.label: The contoured couch
callouts.note: Moulded individually to each astronaut's body, lying on his back, to spread up to eight times his own weight during launch and re-entry.

callouts.label: Instrument panel
callouts.note: Around 120 controls, switches and fuses within arm's reach. The astronaut could fly the capsule's attitude manually -- which Glenn and Carpenter both had to do.

callouts.label: 2.8 cubic metres of cabin
callouts.note: The whole habitable volume, roughly the inside of a telephone box. Astronauts said you did not get into a Mercury capsule, you put it on.

callouts.label: Recovery and antenna section
callouts.note: The narrow cylinder at the top: antennas, and the main and reserve parachutes that brought the capsule down into the Atlantic.

callouts.label: Escape tower attachment
callouts.note: A solid-fuelled tower bolted here could pull the capsule clear of an exploding rocket in a second. It was jettisoned once the booster was safely away.

cutaways.title: Soyuz: three modules, one of which comes home
cutaways.note: A NASA rendering with the descent module picked out solid and the rest of the spacecraft ghosted. There are no labels of its own, so all six points are ours. The docking end is at the lower left.

callouts.label: Docking probe
callouts.note: The probe that engages the station's cone, then retracts to pull the two together and seal the hatch.

callouts.label: Orbital module
callouts.note: Five cubic metres of extra room used in flight for work, sleep and the toilet. It is jettisoned before re-entry and burns up, which is why it does not need a heat shield.

callouts.label: Descent module
callouts.note: The solid shape: the only part that returns, 3.5 cubic metres for three suited crew. After Soyuz 11 killed its crew through a leaking valve, nobody has flown a Soyuz re-entry without a pressure suit.

callouts.label: Service module
callouts.note: Engines, propellant, oxygen and the radiator. Also jettisoned before re-entry.

callouts.label: Solar arrays
callouts.note: A 10.7-metre span, giving the spacecraft independent power for up to several days of free flight before it reaches the station.

callouts.label: The second array
callouts.note: Soyuz has flown since 1967 in a continuously revised form; the three-module layout has never changed, because splitting the habitable volume from the part that must survive re-entry saves a great deal of heat shield.

cutaways.title: Salyut 1, the first space station
cutaways.note: A line drawing from NASA Reference Publication 1357, a public-domain study of Soviet space stations. It has no labels of its own; the five points are ours. A Soyuz ferry is drawn approaching at the upper right.

callouts.label: Transfer compartment and docking port
callouts.note: The only way in. Soyuz 10 reached this port in April 1971 but could not achieve a hard dock, and its crew had to come home without entering.

callouts.label: Solar arrays
callouts.note: Two pairs, one at each end of the station -- an arrangement borrowed from the Soyuz spacecraft that Salyut was partly built from.

callouts.label: Work compartment
callouts.note: Ninety-nine cubic metres of living and working volume for three people, in two sections of different diameter. Soyuz 11's crew lived here for 23 days.

callouts.label: Service and propulsion module
callouts.note: Engines and propellant for raising the orbit, and for the final burn that brought the station down over the Pacific in October 1971.

callouts.label: A Soyuz ferry
callouts.note: The station had no launcher of its own and no way to resupply itself: everything and everyone arrived by Soyuz, and a second docking port only appeared with Salyut 6 in 1977.

cutaways.title: International Space Station configuration
cutaways.note: NASA's own configuration diagram for December 2022, labelled module by module at source. The station changes shape with every visiting vehicle and reconfiguration, so any such drawing is a snapshot: this one is the configuration our scale plate is drawn from.

cutaways.title: Mir, module by module
cutaways.note: A labelled configuration diagram of Mir in its final form, contributed to Wikimedia Commons under a share-alike licence. Six modules were added to the core over ten years, each docked and then swung to a radial port by an arm -- the method the ISS inherited.

cutaways.title: Vostok
cutaways.note: A labelled diagram of the spacecraft Gagarin flew, contributed to Commons under a share-alike licence. The pressurised sphere is the whole crew compartment; the cone below it is the equipment module, jettisoned before re-entry.

cutaways.title: Hubble Space Telescope
cutaways.note: A NASA Goddard cutaway showing the instrument bays behind the 2.4-metre mirror, labelled at source. Every one of those instruments was designed to be swapped by astronauts in gloves -- which is why Hubble is the only telescope that has been upgraded five times in orbit.

cutaways.title: Webb's optical layout
cutaways.note: A NASA diagram of the light path through the telescope, with its labels removed. The points are ours.

callouts.label: Primary mirror, 6.5 m
callouts.note: Eighteen hexagonal beryllium segments coated in gold, folded for launch and aligned in orbit to within a fraction of a wavelength of light.

callouts.label: Secondary mirror
callouts.note: Held out in front on a deployable tripod; it folds flat against the primary for launch.

callouts.label: Instrument module
callouts.note: Four instruments behind the mirror, working in the infrared at about 40 degrees above absolute zero.

callouts.label: The sunshield side
callouts.note: Five kapton layers the size of a tennis court hold a temperature difference of about 300 degrees across the spacecraft. Without them the telescope would see only its own heat.

cutaways.title: Explorer 1
cutaways.note: NASA's own characteristics drawing of America's first satellite, labelled at source. The fourth stage of the launch vehicle stayed attached and is part of the 2.03-metre length.

cutaways.title: Voyager
cutaways.note: A NASA/JPL structural diagram of the Voyager spacecraft, labelled at source. The 3.7-metre dish, the boom carrying the radioisotope generators and the instrument scan platform are the three things that define its shape.

cutaways.title: Starship and Super Heavy, inside
cutaways.note: A Federal Aviation Administration drawing from the Starship launch licensing documents -- a US-government work and so public domain. It shows the tank layout of both stages, labelled at source.

cutaways.title: Tiangong configuration
cutaways.note: A labelled configuration diagram of the completed Chinese station, contributed to Commons under a share-alike licence: the Tianhe core with the Wentian and Mengtian laboratories docked radially, plus the ports for Shenzhou crew ferries and Tianzhou cargo ships.
